questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Iodine needed to make the daily thyroxine output, and the disorder caused by iodine deficiency
questions.question: The thyroid gland of an adult secretes about 80 µg of thyroxine (T₄) per day. One molecule of thyroxine contains four iodine atoms, and its molar mass is 777 g mol⁻¹ (I = 127). Assuming that none of the iodine is recycled, what is the minimum daily intake of iodine needed to make this thyroxine, and which disorder appears when dietary iodine stays too low?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) About 52 µg; goitre.
Concept: Thyroxine (tetraiodothyronine, T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃) are iodine-containing hormones of the thyroid follicles. Iodine is essential for their synthesis. When dietary iodine is too low, little hormone is made, TSH from the pituitary stays high, and the thyroid enlarges (goitre).
Given: 80 µg T₄ per day; M(T₄) = 777 g mol⁻¹; 4 I atoms per molecule; I = 127.
Formula/Principle: mass of iodine = mass of T₄ × (4 × 127)/777.
Step 1: Mass fraction of iodine in T₄ = 508/777 = 0.654.
Step 2: Iodine needed = 80 µg × 0.654 ≈ 52 µg per day.
Why: About two-thirds of the mass of thyroxine is iodine, so 80 µg of hormone carries about 52 µg of iodine. Low iodine lowers hormone output, the negative feedback on TSH is lost, and continued TSH stimulation makes the gland grow.
Why not the others: (A) 39 µg uses three iodine atoms per molecule (that of T₃), not four. (B) Acromegaly comes from excess growth hormone in adults, not from iodine deficiency. (D) It treats the whole mass of thyroxine as iodine.
Key point: T₄ has 4 iodine atoms (about 65 % of its mass); iodine deficiency → low T₄, high TSH → goitre.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Sequence of events from megaspore mother cell to the seven-celled embryo sac
questions.question:
The following events take place inside the ovule of a typical angiosperm (Polygonum type).
P: The nucleus of the functional megaspore undergoes three successive free-nuclear mitoses.
Q: The megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis.
R: One cell of the nucellus near the micropyle differentiates as the megaspore mother cell.
S: Three of the four megaspores degenerate.
T: Cell walls form, giving a seven-celled, eight-nucleate embryo sac.
Which is the correct order?
options: A) R → Q → S → P → T
B) R → P → Q → S → T
C) Q → R → S → P → T
D) R → Q → P → S → T
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) R → Q → S → P → T.
Concept: Megasporogenesis is the formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell (MMC) by meiosis. Megagametogenesis is the development of the functional megaspore into the female gametophyte (embryo sac) by mitosis.
Why: First, a diploid MMC differentiates in the nucellus (R). It divides by meiosis to give four haploid megaspores (Q). Usually only one megaspore is functional and the other three degenerate (S). The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically three times without wall formation, giving 2, 4 and then 8 free nuclei (P). Finally, walls form: three antipodal cells, the egg apparatus (egg and two synergids) and a large central cell with two polar nuclei — seven cells and eight nuclei (T).
Why not the others: (B) Free-nuclear mitoses cannot come before meiosis; they happen in the haploid functional megaspore. (C) The MMC must be formed before it can undergo meiosis. (D) Three megaspores degenerate before the functional one starts its mitoses.
Key point: MMC (2n) → meiosis → 4 megaspores (n) → 1 functional → 3 mitoses → 8 nuclei → 7 cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reason for unequal cytoplasmic division in oogenesis compared with spermatogenesis
questions.question: In humans, one primary spermatocyte gives four spermatids of equal size, but one primary oocyte gives only one large ovum and small polar bodies. Which statement correctly explains this difference and its importance?
options: A) Polar bodies receive all the replicated chromosomes, so the ovum keeps the unreplicated set
B) The oocyte skips meiosis II, so the polar bodies are diploid while the ovum is haploid
C) Polar bodies are made by extra mitotic divisions after meiosis to remove surplus cytoplasm from the ovum

D) Cytokinesis is unequal in both meiotic divisions, so the chromosome number is halved normally while almost all the cytoplasm, with its stored food, organelles and mRNAs, stays in one cell that supports the early embryo
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cytokinesis is unequal in both meiotic divisions, so the chromosome number is halved normally while almost all the cytoplasm, with its stored food, organelles and mRNAs, stays in one cell that supports the early embryo.
Concept: In oogenesis, meiosis I of the primary oocyte gives a large secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body. Meiosis II (completed after the sperm enters) gives the large ovum and a second polar body. Nuclear division is equal; cytoplasmic division is not.
Why: The chromosomes separate exactly as in any meiosis, so the ovum is haploid like each spermatid. But the cleavage furrow forms near the surface, so the oocyte keeps nearly all the cytoplasm. Until the embryo implants and gets food from the mother, early cleavages depend on these stored materials. A sperm, in contrast, needs to be small and motile, so equal division into four is suitable.
Why not the others: (A) Chromosomes are shared equally at each division; the polar body is genetically a sister product, not a store of extra chromosomes. (B) Meiosis II does occur (after sperm entry), and polar bodies are haploid. (C) Polar bodies are products of the two meiotic divisions themselves, not of extra mitoses.
Key point: Oogenesis → equal chromosome division but unequal cytokinesis → one large ovum + polar bodies.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Gene order on a chromosome from recombination frequencies, and the expected distance of the outer genes
questions.question:
Test crosses give the following recombination frequencies between pairs of linked genes on one chromosome.

Gene pair | Recombination frequency
A–B | 8 %
B–C | 12 %
A–C | 20 %
A–D | 5 %
B–D | 13 %

What is the order of the four genes, and about how far apart (in map units) do D and C lie on the map?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) D–A–B–C; about 25 map units.
Concept: The frequency of recombination between two linked genes increases with the distance between them, so it can be used to map genes (Sturtevant). One map unit (centimorgan) corresponds to 1 % recombination. Distances along a line add up.
Why: A–C (20) = A–B (8) + B–C (12), so B lies between A and C. B–D (13) = A–D (5) + A–B (8), so A lies between D and B. The order is therefore D–A–B–C, and the map distance D–C = 5 + 8 + 12 = 25 map units. (Over long distances the measured frequency may be a little smaller than the sum because of double crossovers.)
Why not the others: (A) If D lay between A and B, then B–D would be 8 − 5 = 3, not 13. (C) 13 is the B–D distance, not D–C. (D) A–D is only 5 %, so D cannot lie beyond C at the other end.
Key point: Additive distances fix the order: the middle gene's two distances add up to the distance between the outer genes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Order of events in bacterial transcription and the direction in which the template is read
questions.question:
The following events occur during transcription of a gene in a bacterium.
P: The σ (sigma) factor is released from the enzyme.
Q: RNA polymerase holoenzyme binds the promoter.
R: At the terminator, the ρ (rho) factor helps release the RNA and the polymerase.
S: The DNA is unwound locally and the first few phosphodiester bonds of the RNA are formed.
T: The core enzyme moves along the template, adding ribonucleotides.
Which option gives the correct order and the direction in which the template strand is read?
options: A) Q → S → P → T → R; template read 3′ → 5′
B) Q → S → P → T → R; template read 5′ → 3′
C) S → Q → P → T → R; template read 3′ → 5′
D) Q → P → S → T → R; template read 3′ → 5′
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Q → S → P → T → R; template read 3′ → 5′.
Concept: Bacterial transcription has three stages: initiation, elongation and termination. A single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase associates transiently with the σ factor for initiation and with the ρ factor for termination. RNA is made in the 5′ → 3′ direction, so the antiparallel template strand is read 3′ → 5′.
Why: The holoenzyme (core + σ) recognises and binds the promoter (Q). It opens the DNA and joins the first few nucleotides (S). σ is then released (P), and the core enzyme elongates the RNA along the template (T). At the terminator, ρ helps release the RNA and the enzyme (R).
Why not the others: (B) Nucleotides are added to the 3′ end of the growing RNA, so the template must be read 3′ → 5′, not 5′ → 3′. (C) The DNA is unwound at the promoter only after the enzyme has bound it. (D) σ is needed for initiation, so it leaves only after RNA synthesis has begun.
Key point: σ for initiation, ρ for termination; RNA grows 5′ → 3′ on a template read 3′ → 5′.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Effect of different point mutations, using the degeneracy of the genetic code
questions.question: Part of an mRNA reads 5′-AUG GCU UCA GGA UAA-3′. GCU and GCC both code for alanine, and UAA is a stop codon. Which change in the corresponding gene is most likely to leave the protein unchanged?
options: A) Deletion of the first U of the third codon
B) Insertion of one G just after the start codon
C) A change that turns GCU into GCC
D) A change that turns UCA into UAA
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A change that turns GCU into GCC.
Concept: The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are coded by more than one codon, and the codons for one amino acid often differ only in the third base. A point mutation that changes a codon into another codon for the same amino acid is silent.
Why: GCU → GCC still codes for alanine, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged. The reading frame is not changed because one base replaces another.
Why not the others: (A) Deleting one base shifts the reading frame (frameshift), so every codon after it is read differently. (B) Inserting one base also causes a frameshift from that point. (D) UCA (serine) → UAA (stop) is a nonsense mutation and shortens the protein.
Key point: Silent substitution (same amino acid) < missense < nonsense/frameshift in effect.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ranking three populations by heterozygote frequency under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
questions.question: Three large, randomly mating populations are each in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium for a gene with alleles A and a. The frequency of the recessive phenotype (aa) is 0.01 in population P, 0.25 in population Q and 0.64 in population R. Which is the correct order of the frequency of heterozygotes (Aa)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Q > R > P.
Concept: In Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium the genotype frequencies are p² (AA), 2pq (Aa) and q² (aa), where p + q = 1. The heterozygote frequency 2pq is greatest (0.5) when p = q = 0.5.
Given: q² = 0.01 (P), 0.25 (Q), 0.64 (R).
Formula/Principle: q = √(q²); p = 1 − q; heterozygotes = 2pq.
Step 1: P: q = 0.1, p = 0.9, 2pq = 0.18.
Step 2: Q: q = 0.5, p = 0.5, 2pq = 0.50; R: q = 0.8, p = 0.2, 2pq = 0.32.
Why: The order is Q (0.50) > R (0.32) > P (0.18). Q has equal allele frequencies, which gives the largest 2pq. R and P are on opposite sides of 0.5, and R (q = 0.8) is closer to 0.5 than P (q = 0.1).
Why not the others: (A) This is the order of the recessive phenotype, not of heterozygotes. (C) It reverses the true order. (D) P has the most unequal allele frequencies, so it has the fewest heterozygotes.
Key point: 2pq is largest when p = q; the further q is from 0.5, the fewer heterozygotes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Order of events in the primary and secondary immune responses after vaccination
questions.question:
A person receives a vaccine and, months later, meets the same pathogen. Consider these events.
P: Helper T cells activate naïve B cells that have recognised the vaccine antigen.
Q: Plasma cells produce antibodies at a modest level (primary response).
R: Antibody levels fall, but memory B and T cells persist.
S: On infection, memory cells proliferate rapidly.
T: A large amount of antibody appears within a few days (secondary response).
Which order is correct?
options: A) P → R → Q → S → T
B) S → P → Q → R → T
C) P → Q → S → R → T
D) P → Q → R → S → T
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P → Q → R → S → T.
Concept: The first encounter with an antigen gives a primary response of low intensity. It also produces memory B and T cells. A later encounter with the same antigen gives a secondary (anamnestic) response, which is faster and much stronger. Vaccination uses this immunological memory.
Why: After vaccination, helper T cells activate B cells (P), which form plasma cells secreting antibody (Q). As the antigen is removed, antibody levels fall, but memory cells remain (R). When the pathogen enters, the memory cells recognise it and multiply quickly (S), giving a high level of antibody within days (T), before disease can develop.
Why not the others: (A) Memory cells are made during the primary response, after antibody production starts; antibody levels fall later. (B) Memory cells cannot respond before the first exposure has made them. (C) The fall in antibody and persistence of memory cells come before the later infection.
Key point: Primary response → memory cells → faster, stronger secondary response (basis of vaccination).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Starting copy number and amplification factor from PCR data
questions.question:
A PCR is run in which every cycle has the same efficiency. Samples are taken at three points, and the number of copies of the target DNA is measured.

Cycle number | Copies of target
10 | \(1.02\times10^{5}\)
15 | \(3.28\times10^{6}\)
20 | \(1.05\times10^{8}\)

How many target copies were present at the start, and by what factor does the number increase in each cycle?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) About 100; 2 per cycle.
Concept: In each PCR cycle (denaturation, primer annealing, extension by a thermostable DNA polymerase), each double-stranded target can be copied once, so with full efficiency the number of copies doubles: \(N=N_0\times2^{n}\).
Why: Over 5 cycles the number rises by \(3.28\times10^{6}/1.02\times10^{5}\approx32=2^{5}\), and again \(1.05\times10^{8}/3.28\times10^{6}\approx32\). So the factor per cycle is 2. Then \(N_0=1.02\times10^{5}/2^{10}=1.02\times10^{5}/1024\approx100\).
Why not the others: (A) 1000 copies would give \(1.02\times10^{6}\) after 10 cycles, ten times the measured value. (B) 32 is the increase over five cycles, not one. (D) A factor of 4 is impossible, because one cycle at most doubles the target; also \(10\times4^{10}\approx1.05\times10^{7}\), which does not match.
Key point: Ideal PCR: \(N=N_0\,2^{n}\); compare readings a few cycles apart to find the factor.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting a removal experiment with two barnacle species: fundamental and realised niche
questions.question: On a rocky sea shore, barnacle species X lives only in the upper intertidal zone and the larger species Y only in the lower zone, although larvae of X settle in both zones. When Y is removed from part of the lower zone, X survives and grows there. When X is removed from the upper zone, Y still does not spread upwards, because it dies of drying when exposed at low tide. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: A) The lower limit of X is set by competition with Y, so the realised niche of X is narrower than its fundamental niche; the upper limit of Y is set by a physical factor
B) Both species are limited only by competition with each other
C) X excludes Y from the upper zone by competition
D) Y feeds on X, so the distribution of X is set by predation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The lower limit of X is set by competition with Y, so the realised niche of X is narrower than its fundamental niche; the upper limit of Y is set by a physical factor.
Concept: Interspecific competition can restrict a species to only part of the range it could occupy. The fundamental niche is the whole range of conditions a species can tolerate; the realised niche is the part it actually occupies in the presence of competitors. Connell's study of barnacles on the Scottish coast is a classic field example.
Why: X can live in the lower zone when Y is absent, so its absence there in nature is caused by Y (competitive exclusion, for example by crowding out or overgrowing). Removing X does not let Y move up, so Y's upper limit is set by drying out (a physical factor), not by X.
Why not the others: (B) Y does not spread upwards even without X, so the upper limit of Y is not set by competition. (C) The experiment shows the opposite: removing X has no effect on Y. (D) Both are filter-feeding barnacles; no feeding of one on the other is described, and X thrives in the lower zone only when Y is removed.
Key point: Removal experiments show competition when the other species expands into the vacated zone.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Matching members of Monera and Protista with distinctive features
questions.question:
Match each organism with its distinctive feature.
Organisms: P Nostoc; Q Euglena; R a diatom; S Mycoplasma.
Features: (1) no cell wall; (2) heterocysts that fix nitrogen; (3) a flexible protein-rich pellicle instead of a cell wall; (4) silica-containing walls that build up as diatomaceous earth.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P-2, Q-3, R-4, S-1.
Concept: Kingdom Monera has prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria and mycoplasma; kingdom Protista has unicellular eukaryotes such as euglenoids and chrysophytes (diatoms).
Why: Nostoc is a filamentous cyanobacterium with heterocysts that fix nitrogen (P-2). Euglena is a euglenoid with a flexible pellicle and no cell wall of cellulose (Q-3). Diatoms have walls containing silica, which form two overlapping halves and accumulate as diatomaceous earth (R-4). Mycoplasma has no cell wall at all and is among the smallest living cells (S-1).
Why not the others: (A) Nostoc has a cell wall; heterocysts are not found in Mycoplasma. (B) Euglena does not have silica walls, and diatoms do not have a pellicle. (C) Nostoc has no pellicle and Euglena no heterocysts.
Key point: Heterocysts → cyanobacteria; pellicle → euglenoids; silica → diatoms; no wall → Mycoplasma.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing levels of organisation, symmetry, body cavity and special cells from Porifera to Aschelminthes
questions.question: Which comparison between animal phyla is correct?
options: A) Porifera and Cnidaria both have a tissue level of organisation
B) Ctenophora and Cnidaria are both diploblastic and radially symmetrical, but only ctenophores have comb plates and only cnidarians have cnidoblasts
C) Platyhelminthes and Aschelminthes are both pseudocoelomate
D) Aschelminthes excrete through flame cells, while Platyhelminthes have an excretory tube that opens through a pore
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ctenophora and Cnidaria are both diploblastic and radially symmetrical, but only ctenophores have comb plates and only cnidarians have cnidoblasts.
Concept: The early animal phyla differ in level of organisation (cellular, tissue, organ), germ layers (diploblastic or triploblastic), symmetry and body cavity (acoelomate, pseudocoelomate, coelomate), and each has some special structures.
Why: Cnidarians (e.g. Hydra) and ctenophores (e.g. Pleurobrachia) are both diploblastic, radially symmetrical animals with tissue-level organisation. Ctenophores move with eight rows of ciliated comb plates; cnidarians have stinging cnidoblasts on their tentacles.
Why not the others: (A) Sponges (Porifera) have a cellular level of organisation; cells do not form true tissues. (C) Flatworms are acoelomate; roundworms (Aschelminthes) are pseudocoelomate. (D) The features are swapped: flame cells are found in flatworms, and roundworms have an excretory tube opening through an excretory pore.
Key point: Porifera cellular; Cnidaria and Ctenophora diploblastic, radial; flatworms acoelomate with flame cells; roundworms pseudocoelomate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Identifying mitochondria, chloroplasts and 80S ribosomes from their properties
questions.question:
Three cell components of a green plant cell, X, Y and Z, have the properties listed.

Component | Membranes around it | Own DNA | Ribosomes inside | Other feature
X | 2 | circular | 70S | inner membrane folded into cristae
Y | 2 | circular | 70S | stacked membrane sacs (grana) with pigments
Z | none | none | — | made of a large (60S) and a small (40S) subunit

Which identification is correct?
options: A) X mitochondrion, Y chloroplast, Z cytoplasmic 80S ribosome
B) X chloroplast, Y mitochondrion, Z 70S ribosome
C) X mitochondrion, Y chloroplast, Z 70S ribosome
D) X Golgi body, Y chloroplast, Z centriole
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) X mitochondrion, Y chloroplast, Z cytoplasmic 80S ribosome.
Concept: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are double-membrane-bound organelles with their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes (semi-autonomous). Ribosomes are not bound by membranes; eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S), and prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S (50S + 30S).
Why: Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, so X is a mitochondrion. Grana are stacks of thylakoids containing chlorophyll, so Y is a chloroplast. Z has no membrane and subunits of 60S and 40S, so it is an 80S ribosome of the cytoplasm.
Why not the others: (B) Cristae belong to mitochondria and grana to chloroplasts, so X and Y are swapped. (C) 60S + 40S subunits make an 80S ribosome, not a 70S one (S values do not add). (D) The Golgi body has a single membrane and no DNA; a centriole is made of microtubules, not ribosomal subunits.
Key point: Mitochondria and chloroplasts: two membranes, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes; cytoplasmic ribosomes: 80S = 60S + 40S.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Structural and chemical differences between DNA and RNA, and the scope of Chargaff's rule
questions.question:
Consider these statements about nucleic acids.
I. RNA is readily hydrolysed in dilute alkali, but DNA is not, because ribose has a 2′-OH group.
II. Thymine is 5-methyluracil.
III. In any double-stranded DNA, A + G = C + T, but A + T need not equal G + C.
IV. In any single-stranded RNA, the amount of adenine equals the amount of uracil.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) I, II and III.
Concept: DNA contains deoxyribose and thymine; RNA contains ribose and uracil. In double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and G with C, so purines equal pyrimidines (Chargaff's rule). Base pairing rules do not fix the composition of a single strand.
Why: I: the 2′-OH of ribose can attack the neighbouring phosphodiester bond, so RNA is chemically more reactive and is broken down by alkali; this is one reason DNA is the more stable genetic material. II: thymine is uracil with a methyl group at C-5. III: A = T and G = C give A + G = C + T, but the proportion of A–T to G–C pairs varies between species.
Why not the others: (A) It leaves out III, which follows from base pairing. (B) It leaves out I, which is correct. (D) IV is false: a single strand has no partner strand, so A and U need not be equal.
Key point: Chargaff's equalities apply to double-stranded DNA only; RNA's 2′-OH makes it less stable than DNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ethanol as a competitive inhibitor in methanol poisoning: effect on Km and Vmax
questions.question: In the liver, the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase converts methanol into poisonous formaldehyde. The same enzyme also acts on ethanol. Patients with methanol poisoning are sometimes given large doses of ethanol. Which explanation and which change in the kinetics of methanol oxidation are correct?
options: A) Ethanol binds the enzyme at a separate site and lowers Vmax for methanol, while Km is unchanged
B) Ethanol denatures the enzyme permanently, so no methanol is oxidised
C) Ethanol reacts with formaldehyde and makes it harmless, while the enzyme is unaffected
D) Ethanol competes with methanol for the active site, so the apparent Km for methanol rises while Vmax is unchanged, and much methanol is excreted unchanged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ethanol competes with methanol for the active site, so the apparent Km for methanol rises while Vmax is unchanged, and much methanol is excreted unchanged.
Concept: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and binds reversibly to the active site. It raises the apparent Km (more substrate is needed to reach half the maximum rate) but does not change Vmax, because enough substrate can still outcompete it.
Why: Ethanol is also a substrate of the enzyme and occupies the active site. With a large excess of ethanol, little methanol is converted to formaldehyde at any time, so the toxic product forms slowly and the unchanged methanol can be lost through the kidneys and lungs.
Why not the others: (A) Binding at a separate site and lowering Vmax describes non-competitive inhibition. (B) Ethanol does not destroy the enzyme; it is itself converted by the enzyme. (C) The protection comes from reduced formation of formaldehyde, not from a reaction with it.
Key point: Competitive inhibitor → same active site, Km increases, Vmax unchanged.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: ATP and NADPH used in the Calvin cycle to make one molecule of sucrose
questions.question: In a C₃ plant, how many molecules of ATP and NADPH are used in the Calvin cycle to fix the carbon dioxide needed for one molecule of sucrose (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁)? Ignore the energy used in joining the two hexose units.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 36 ATP and 24 NADPH.
Concept: In the Calvin cycle, each CO₂ fixed by RuBisCO needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH: 2 ATP and 2 NADPH for reduction of 3-PGA to triose phosphate, and 1 ATP for regeneration of RuBP. Six turns (6 CO₂) make one hexose using 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
Given: sucrose has 12 carbon atoms; per CO₂: 3 ATP, 2 NADPH.
Formula/Principle: number of turns = number of carbon atoms in the product; ATP = 3 × turns; NADPH = 2 × turns.
Step 1: 12 carbon atoms → 12 CO₂ fixed → 12 turns of the cycle.
Step 2: ATP = 3 × 12 = 36; NADPH = 2 × 12 = 24.
Why: Sucrose is made from one glucose and one fructose, so it needs twice the requirement for one hexose. The ATP : NADPH ratio stays 3 : 2.
Why not the others: (A) This is the requirement for one hexose, not for a disaccharide of two hexoses. (C) The ratio of ATP to NADPH is reversed. (D) It uses 3 NADPH per CO₂; only 2 NADPH are used per CO₂.
Key point: Calvin cycle: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂; one hexose = 18 ATP + 12 NADPH.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Exponential growth of a callus formed by dedifferentiation: relative growth rate and later mass
questions.question: A leaf explant on a nutrient medium with auxin and cytokinin forms a callus, whose mass grows exponentially from 0.50 g to 4.0 g in 15 days. If it continues to grow in the same way, what will its mass be after 20 days from the start, and what is its relative growth rate? (ln 2 = 0.693)
options: A) About 5.2 g; 0.23 g per day
B) About 16 g; about 0.28 per day
C) About 8.0 g; about 0.14 per day
D) About 8.0 g; about 0.70 per day
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) About 8.0 g; about 0.14 per day.
Concept: Formation of a callus from mature, non-dividing cells is dedifferentiation: the cells regain the ability to divide. In exponential (geometric) growth, \(W_t=W_0e^{rt}\), where r is the relative growth rate (growth per unit mass per unit time).
Given: \(W_0=0.50\) g; \(W_{15}=4.0\) g; exponential growth.
Formula/Principle: \(W_t=W_0e^{rt}\); doubling time \(=\ln2/r\).
Step 1: 4.0/0.50 = 8 = 2³, so the mass doubles three times in 15 days: doubling time = 5 days.
Step 2: \(r=\ln2/5=0.693/5\approx0.14\) per day; 20 days = 4 doublings, so \(W_{20}=0.50\times2^{4}=8.0\) g.
Why: In geometric growth the mass increases by the same factor in equal times, so the 15-day factor of 8 means a factor of 2 every 5 days. Later, shoots or roots formed from the callus would be redifferentiation.
Why not the others: (A) It assumes arithmetic (linear) growth of 3.5 g in 15 days. (B) 16 g corresponds to five doublings, i.e. 25 days. (D) 0.70 is ln 2, not ln 2 divided by the doubling time.
Key point: Exponential growth: equal factors in equal times; \(r=\ln2/\text{doubling time}\).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ranking lung capacities from the four primary lung volumes
questions.question: For a healthy adult, tidal volume = 500 mL, inspiratory reserve volume = 2500 mL, expiratory reserve volume = 1000 mL and residual volume = 1200 mL. Consider these capacities: P inspiratory capacity; Q functional residual capacity; R expiratory capacity; S vital capacity. Which is the correct increasing order?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) R < Q < P < S.
Concept: Lung capacities are sums of primary volumes: inspiratory capacity IC = TV + IRV; expiratory capacity EC = TV + ERV; functional residual capacity FRC = ERV + RV; vital capacity VC = ERV + TV + IRV.
Given: TV = 500, IRV = 2500, ERV = 1000, RV = 1200 (mL).
Formula/Principle: add the volumes that make up each capacity.
Step 1: R (EC) = 500 + 1000 = 1500 mL; Q (FRC) = 1000 + 1200 = 2200 mL.
Step 2: P (IC) = 500 + 2500 = 3000 mL; S (VC) = 1000 + 500 + 2500 = 4000 mL.
Why: The order is 1500 < 2200 < 3000 < 4000, i.e. R < Q < P < S. Vital capacity includes every volume except the residual volume, so it is the largest of these four.
Why not the others: (B) FRC (2200) is larger than EC (1500). (C) IC (3000) is larger than FRC (2200). (D) VC contains IC plus ERV, so VC must exceed IC.
Key point: IC = TV + IRV; EC = TV + ERV; FRC = ERV + RV; VC = TV + IRV + ERV.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: State of the heart valves during ventricular systole and the pressure differences that cause it
questions.question: During ventricular systole (after the initial short phase in which all valves are shut), which description of the heart valves and its cause is correct?
options: A) The atrioventricular valves are open because atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, and the semilunar valves are closed

B) The tricuspid and bicuspid valves are closed because ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, and the semilunar valves are open because ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the pulmonary artery and aorta
C) All four valves stay closed during the whole of systole
D) All four valves are open so that blood can move freely through the heart
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The tricuspid and bicuspid valves are closed because ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, and the semilunar valves are open because ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the pulmonary artery and aorta.
Concept: Heart valves open and close passively according to the pressure on their two sides, and they allow flow in one direction only. This keeps the double circulation one-way: right ventricle → lungs, left ventricle → body.
Why: When the ventricles contract, ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure and the atrioventricular valves close (first heart sound, "lub"). When ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the pulmonary artery and aorta, the semilunar valves open and blood is ejected. At the end of systole the semilunar valves close ("dub").
Why not the others: (A) This describes ventricular diastole, when the ventricles fill. (C) All valves are shut only for a short time at the start of systole; blood could not be ejected if they stayed shut. (D) Open atrioventricular valves during systole would let blood flow back into the atria.
Key point: Systole: AV valves closed, semilunar valves open; diastole: the reverse.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the composition of plasma, glomerular filtrate and urine
questions.question:
The table gives the concentration (g per 100 mL) of some substances in the blood plasma, the glomerular filtrate and the urine of a healthy person.

Substance | Plasma | Glomerular filtrate | Urine
Protein | 8.0 | 0 | 0
Glucose | 0.10 | 0.10 | 0
Urea | 0.03 | 0.03 | 2.0
Sodium ions | 0.30 | 0.30 | 0.35

Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) Glucose is not filtered at the glomerulus
B) Proteins are filtered and then completely reabsorbed in the tubule
C) Urea is not filtered; it enters the urine only by secretion
D) Proteins are not filtered; glucose is filtered and completely reabsorbed; urea becomes about 67 times more concentrated, mainly because most of the filtered water is reabsorbed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Proteins are not filtered; glucose is filtered and completely reabsorbed; urea becomes about 67 times more concentrated, mainly because most of the filtered water is reabsorbed.
Concept: Glomerular filtration is ultrafiltration: blood cells and plasma proteins stay in the blood, while small solutes pass into the filtrate at the same concentration as in plasma. The tubule then reabsorbs useful substances (glucose, amino acids, much Na⁺ and about 99 % of the water).
Why: Protein is 8.0 in plasma but 0 in filtrate, so it is not filtered. Glucose is 0.10 in filtrate but 0 in urine, so it is entirely reabsorbed (in the proximal convoluted tubule). Urea is at the same concentration in plasma and filtrate, so it is freely filtered; its concentration in urine is 2.0/0.03 ≈ 67 times higher because water is removed from the tubular fluid.
Why not the others: (A) Glucose has the same concentration in filtrate as in plasma, so it is filtered. (B) Protein is already 0 in the filtrate, so it never enters the tubule. (C) Urea is present in the filtrate at the plasma concentration, so it is filtered.
Key point: Filtrate ≈ protein-free plasma; glucose fully reabsorbed; urea concentrated by water reabsorption.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Lattice enthalpy of sodium chloride from a Born–Haber cycle using atomisation, ionisation, electron gain and formation enthalpies
questions.question: Use the following data (kJ mol⁻¹) for a Born–Haber cycle: enthalpy of atomisation (sublimation) of Na(s) +108; first ionisation enthalpy of Na(g) +496; bond dissociation enthalpy of \(\ce{Cl2(g)}\) +242; electron gain enthalpy of Cl(g) −349; standard enthalpy of formation of NaCl(s) −411. What is the lattice enthalpy of NaCl, defined as the enthalpy change for \(\ce{NaCl(s) -> Na+(g) + Cl-(g)}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) +787 kJ mol⁻¹.
Concept: A Born–Haber cycle applies Hess's law to the formation of an ionic solid. The route "elements → gaseous atoms → gaseous ions → solid" must have the same total enthalpy change as the direct formation reaction. The lattice enthalpy (for breaking the lattice into gaseous ions) is positive.
Given: \(\Delta_{\text{sub}}H(\ce{Na})=+108\); IE = +496; \(D(\ce{Cl2})=+242\); \(\Delta_{eg}H(\ce{Cl})=-349\); \(\Delta_fH(\ce{NaCl})=-411\) kJ mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta_fH=\Delta_{\text{sub}}H+\text{IE}+\tfrac12D(\ce{Cl2})+\Delta_{eg}H-\Delta_{\text{lattice}}H\).
Step 1: Only half a mole of \(\ce{Cl2}\) is needed for one mole of Cl atoms: \(\tfrac12\times242=121\) kJ.
Step 2: \(\Delta_{\text{lattice}}H=108+496+121-349-(-411)=+787\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).
Why: Forming gaseous Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from the elements costs 108 + 496 + 121 − 349 = +376 kJ. The solid lies 411 kJ below the elements, so it lies 376 + 411 = 787 kJ below the gaseous ions. This large lattice enthalpy is what makes NaCl stable, although forming the gaseous ions is endothermic.
Why not the others: (A) It leaves out the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond. (B) The sign is that of lattice formation, not of breaking the lattice as defined. (C) It uses the whole bond enthalpy of Cl₂ instead of half.
Key point: Born–Haber: \(\Delta_fH=\text{(atomisation + ionisation + electron gain)}-\Delta_{\text{lattice}}H\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Sign of ΔG for melting of ice below, at and above 273 K from ΔH and ΔS
questions.question: For \(\ce{H2O(s) -> H2O(l)}\), \(\Delta H=+6.01\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\) and \(\Delta S=+22.0\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\); assume both are independent of temperature. What is \(\Delta G\) for melting at 263 K, 273 K and 283 K, respectively, and what follows?
options: A) −0.22, −0.22 and −0.22 kJ mol⁻¹; ice melts at all three temperatures because ΔS > 0
B) +0.22, about 0 and −0.22 kJ mol⁻¹; melting is spontaneous only above about 273 K
C) −0.22, about 0 and +0.22 kJ mol⁻¹; melting is spontaneous only below 273 K
D) +6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ at all three temperatures; melting is never spontaneous
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) +0.22, about 0 and −0.22 kJ mol⁻¹; melting is spontaneous only above about 273 K.
Concept: At constant temperature and pressure a process is spontaneous when \(\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S<0\). This is equivalent to the second law: the total entropy (system + surroundings) increases, with \(\Delta S_{\text{surr}}=-\Delta H/T\).
Given: \(\Delta H=6010\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\); \(\Delta S=22.0\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\); T = 263, 273, 283 K.
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S\).
Step 1: 263 K: \(6010-263\times22.0=6010-5786=+224\ \mathrm J\approx+0.22\) kJ.
Step 2: 273 K: \(6010-6006=+4\ \mathrm J\approx0\); 283 K: \(6010-6226=-216\ \mathrm J\approx-0.22\) kJ.
Why: Melting is endothermic but increases entropy. At low T the \(\Delta H\) term wins (ΔG > 0, water freezes); at high T the \(T\Delta S\) term wins (ΔG < 0, ice melts). At \(T=\Delta H/\Delta S=273\) K the two phases are in equilibrium.
Why not the others: (A) A positive ΔS alone does not decide; ΔG changes with T. (C) The signs are reversed: the \(-T\Delta S\) term becomes more negative as T rises. (D) It ignores the entropy term.
Key point: ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0 → spontaneous only above \(T=\Delta H/\Delta S\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ordering species concentrations in a solution of the weak diprotic acid H2S
questions.question: A 0.10 mol L⁻¹ aqueous solution of \(\ce{H2S}\) is at 298 K. For \(\ce{H2S}\), \(K_{a1}=1.0\times10^{-7}\) and \(K_{a2}=1.3\times10^{-13}\); \(K_w=1.0\times10^{-14}\). Which order of equilibrium concentrations is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \([\ce{H2S}]>[\ce{H+}]\approx[\ce{HS-}]>[\ce{OH-}]>[\ce{S^2-}]\).
Concept: For a weak diprotic acid with \(K_{a2}\ll K_{a1}\), almost all the \(\ce{H+}\) comes from the first step, so \([\ce{H+}]\approx[\ce{HS-}]\). Then the second step gives \([\ce{S^2-}]\approx K_{a2}\), independent of the acid concentration.
Given: c = 0.10 M; \(K_{a1}=1.0\times10^{-7}\); \(K_{a2}=1.3\times10^{-13}\); \(K_w=10^{-14}\).
Formula/Principle: \([\ce{H+}]\approx\sqrt{K_{a1}c}\); \([\ce{S^2-}]=K_{a2}[\ce{HS-}]/[\ce{H+}]\approx K_{a2}\); \([\ce{OH-}]=K_w/[\ce{H+}]\).
Step 1: \([\ce{H+}]\approx[\ce{HS-}]=\sqrt{10^{-7}\times0.10}=1.0\times10^{-4}\) M; \([\ce{H2S}]\approx0.10\) M.
Step 2: \([\ce{S^2-}]\approx1.3\times10^{-13}\) M; \([\ce{OH-}]=10^{-14}/10^{-4}=1.0\times10^{-10}\) M.
Why: So 0.10 > 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ > 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ > 1.3 × 10⁻¹³. Only 0.1 % of the acid ionises, and the sulfide ion is the least abundant species, even scarcer than hydroxide.
Why not the others: (B) \(\ce{S^2-}\) is formed from \(\ce{HS-}\) in the much weaker second step, so it cannot exceed \(\ce{HS-}\). (C) A weak acid is mostly un-ionised, so \([\ce{H2S}]\gg[\ce{H+}]\). (D) It misplaces \(\ce{S^2-}\): \(1.3\times10^{-13}<1.0\times10^{-10}\).
Key point: Weak diprotic acid: \([\ce{H+}]\approx[\ce{HA-}]\approx\sqrt{K_{a1}c}\), and \([\ce{A^2-}]\approx K_{a2}\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the acidity of four salt solutions from hydrolysis of their ions
questions.question: Equal volumes of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ solutions of \(\ce{NH4Cl}\), \(\ce{Na2CO3}\), \(\ce{NaCl}\) and \(\ce{CH3COONH4}\) are tested with universal indicator at 298 K. For \(\ce{CH3COOH}\), \(K_a=1.8\times10^{-5}\); for \(\ce{NH3}\), \(K_b=1.8\times10^{-5}\). Which set of results is expected, in the order given?
options: C) Acidic, basic, neutral, nearly neutral
D) Acidic, neutral, neutral, nearly neutral
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Acidic, basic, neutral, nearly neutral.
Concept: Salt hydrolysis: the cation of a weak base makes a solution acidic, the anion of a weak acid makes it basic, and ions of strong acids and strong bases do not react with water. For a salt of a weak acid and a weak base, \(\text{pH}=7+\tfrac12(\text{p}K_a-\text{p}K_b)\).
Why: \(\ce{NH4+ + H2O <=> NH3 + H3O+}\) makes \(\ce{NH4Cl}\) acidic (pH ≈ 5.1). \(\ce{CO3^2- + H2O <=> HCO3- + OH-}\) makes \(\ce{Na2CO3}\) basic. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ do not hydrolyse, so NaCl is neutral. In \(\ce{CH3COONH4}\) both ions hydrolyse to the same extent because \(K_a=K_b\), so pH ≈ 7 + ½(4.74 − 4.74) = 7.
Why not the others: (A) \(\ce{NH4+}\) is an acid, not a base, so \(\ce{NH4Cl}\) is acidic. (B) For ammonium acetate, the acidity of \(\ce{NH4+}\) is balanced by the basicity of \(\ce{CH3COO-}\). (D) Carbonate is the anion of a weak acid and makes the solution basic.
Key point: Weak-base cation → acidic; weak-acid anion → basic; both with \(K_a=K_b\) → about neutral.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Ordering enthalpies of hydrogenation of alkenes by the number of hyperconjugating α-hydrogens
questions.question: Consider the alkenes P 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, Q 2-methylbut-2-ene, R (E)-but-2-ene and S but-1-ene. Which is the correct increasing order of the magnitude of their enthalpies of hydrogenation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) P < Q < R < S.
Concept: Hyperconjugation is the delocalisation of σ electrons of a C–H bond on a carbon next to the double bond (an α-hydrogen) into the π system. More α-hydrogens mean more hyperconjugative structures and a more stable alkene. A more stable alkene releases less heat when it is hydrogenated.
Why: The α-hydrogens are: P 12 (four CH₃ groups), Q 9 (three CH₃), R 6 (two CH₃), S 2 (one CH₂ of the ethyl group). So stability is P > Q > R > S, and the heat released on hydrogenation is smallest for P and largest for S (about 111, 113, 115 and 127 kJ mol⁻¹).
Why not the others: (A) This is the order of stability written the wrong way; the most stable alkene releases the least heat. (C) Q has more α-hydrogens than R, so it is more stable and releases less heat. (D) P is the most stable and must have the smallest value.
Key point: More α-H → more hyperconjugation → more stable alkene → smaller heat of hydrogenation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linked sequence: acidity of a terminal alkyne, alkylation, and reduction with sodium in liquid ammonia
questions.question: Propyne is treated with sodamide (\(\ce{NaNH2}\)) in liquid ammonia to give X. X reacts with bromoethane to give Y, and Y is reduced with sodium in liquid ammonia to give Z. Which option correctly identifies Y and Z and explains the first step?
options: A) Y is pent-1-yne and Z is pent-1-ene; the first step is an addition of \(\ce{NH2-}\) to the triple bond
B) Y is pent-1-yne and Z is (Z)-pent-1-ene; propyne is more acidic because it has a methyl group
C) Y is pent-2-yne and Z is (Z)-pent-2-ene; the C–H of the terminal alkyne is acidic because carbon is sp³
D) Y is pent-2-yne and Z is (E)-pent-2-ene; the terminal C–H is acidic because the sp carbon has 50 % s character, so \(\ce{NH2-}\) removes the proton
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Y is pent-2-yne and Z is (E)-pent-2-ene; the terminal C–H is acidic because the sp carbon has 50 % s character, so \(\ce{NH2-}\) removes the proton.
Concept: Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic: an sp carbon holds the electron pair of its conjugate base close to the nucleus. They are deprotonated by the stronger base \(\ce{NH2-}\). The alkynide ion is a nucleophile that displaces bromide from a primary alkyl halide. Sodium in liquid ammonia reduces an internal alkyne to the trans (E) alkene.
Why: \(\ce{CH3C#CH + NaNH2 -> CH3C#C^-Na+ + NH3}\) (X). \(\ce{CH3C#C^- + CH3CH2Br -> CH3C#CCH2CH3}\) (Y, pent-2-yne). Na/liquid NH₃ adds two H atoms on opposite sides to give (E)-\(\ce{CH3CH=CHCH2CH3}\) (Z).
Why not the others: (A) \(\ce{NH2-}\) acts as a base and removes the terminal proton; it does not add to the triple bond. (B) The new C–C bond forms at the terminal carbon, so the triple bond ends up at C-2; and the methyl group does not make the C–H acidic. (C) The acidic carbon is sp, not sp³; and Na/NH₃ gives the E isomer (Lindlar catalyst gives Z).
Key point: Terminal alkyne + NaNH₂ → alkynide → alkylation; Na/liquid NH₃ → trans alkene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Applying Hückel's rule to cyclic ions and molecules
questions.question: Which of the following are aromatic: P cyclopentadienyl anion \(\ce{C5H5-}\); Q cycloheptatrienyl (tropylium) cation \(\ce{C7H7+}\); R cyclooctatetraene \(\ce{C8H8}\); S cyclopentadiene \(\ce{C5H6}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P and Q only.
Concept: A species is aromatic if it is cyclic, planar, fully conjugated (every ring atom has a p orbital in the π system) and has (4n + 2) π electrons (Hückel's rule).
Why: P: five sp² carbons, planar, with 6 π electrons (four from two C=C and two from the carbanion lone pair) → aromatic (n = 1). Q: seven sp² carbons, planar, with 6 π electrons (the positive carbon has an empty p orbital) → aromatic.
Why not the others: (B) R has 8 π electrons (4n), and the molecule takes a non-planar tub shape, so it is non-aromatic. (C) S has an sp³ CH₂ group, so the ring is not fully conjugated; R is also not aromatic. (D) It misses P, which also has 6 π electrons in a planar conjugated ring.
Key point: Cyclic + planar + fully conjugated + (4n + 2) π electrons → aromatic.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Total vapour pressure and vapour composition above an ideal benzene–toluene solution
questions.question: At a certain temperature the vapour pressures of pure benzene and pure toluene are 75 torr and 22 torr. A solution is made from 1.0 mol of benzene and 3.0 mol of toluene, and it behaves ideally. The vapour in equilibrium with it is collected and condensed. What is the total vapour pressure, and what is the mole fraction of benzene in the condensed vapour?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 35.3 torr; 0.53.
Concept: Raoult's law for an ideal solution: \(p_i=x_ip_i^\circ\). By Dalton's law, the mole fraction of a component in the vapour is \(y_i=p_i/p_{\text{total}}\). The vapour is richer in the more volatile component.
Given: \(p^\circ_B=75\) torr, \(p^\circ_T=22\) torr; \(n_B=1.0\), \(n_T=3.0\) mol.
Formula/Principle: \(p_{\text{total}}=x_Bp^\circ_B+x_Tp^\circ_T\); \(y_B=x_Bp^\circ_B/p_{\text{total}}\).
Step 1: \(x_B=0.25\), \(x_T=0.75\); \(p_B=18.75\), \(p_T=16.5\) torr; \(p_{\text{total}}=35.25\approx35.3\) torr.
Step 2: \(y_B=18.75/35.25=0.53\).
Why: Benzene is only 25 % of the liquid but 53 % of the vapour, because it is more volatile. This enrichment is the basis of fractional distillation.
Why not the others: (A) 0.25 is the mole fraction of benzene in the liquid, not in the vapour. (B) 48.5 torr is the plain average of the two vapour pressures, ignoring the composition. (D) 0.47 is the mole fraction of toluene in the vapour.
Key point: Vapour is enriched in the more volatile component: \(y_i=x_ip_i^\circ/p_{\text{total}}\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linked use of the Debye–Hückel–Onsager relation: limiting molar conductivity and a prediction at higher concentration
questions.question: For a strong electrolyte, the molar conductivity is \(124.0\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\) at 0.010 mol L⁻¹ and \(118.0\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}}\) at 0.040 mol L⁻¹. Assuming \(\Lambda_m=\Lambda_m^\circ-A\sqrt c\), what are \(\Lambda_m^\circ\) and the expected \(\Lambda_m\) at 0.090 mol L⁻¹ (in S cm² mol⁻¹)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 130; 112.
Concept: For strong electrolytes, molar conductivity decreases slightly with concentration because of interionic attractions, and \(\Lambda_m\) is linear in \(\sqrt c\). The intercept at \(\sqrt c=0\) is the limiting molar conductivity \(\Lambda_m^\circ\).
Given: \(\Lambda_m=124.0\) at \(\sqrt c=0.10\); \(\Lambda_m=118.0\) at \(\sqrt c=0.20\).
Formula/Principle: \(\Lambda_m=\Lambda_m^\circ-A\sqrt c\).
Step 1: \(A=(124.0-118.0)/(0.20-0.10)=60\ \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}\,(mol\,L^{-1})^{-1/2}}\).
Step 2: \(\Lambda_m^\circ=124.0+60\times0.10=130\); at c = 0.090, \(\sqrt c=0.30\): \(\Lambda_m=130-60\times0.30=112\).
Why: The two points fix the straight line; the first answer is its intercept and the second is a point further along it.
Why not the others: (A) It plots \(\Lambda_m\) against c instead of \(\sqrt c\). (B) It takes the value at 0.010 M as the limiting value. (C) It doubles the slope.
Key point: Strong electrolyte: plot \(\Lambda_m\) against \(\sqrt c\); intercept = \(\Lambda_m^\circ\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Order of reaction from the dependence of half-life on initial concentration, and a later time
questions.question:
For the decomposition of A at a fixed temperature, the half-life depends on the initial concentration as shown.

[A]₀ / mol L⁻¹ | t½ / s
0.10 | 40
0.20 | 20
0.40 | 10

What is the order of the reaction, what is k, and how long does it take for [A] to fall from 0.20 mol L⁻¹ to 0.05 mol L⁻¹?
options: A) Second order; 0.25 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; 60 s
C) Zero order; 0.00125 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; 120 s
D) Second order; 0.25 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; 40 s
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Second order; 0.25 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; 60 s.
Concept: Half-life depends on initial concentration differently for each order: zero order \(t_{1/2}\propto[A]_0\); first order \(t_{1/2}\) independent of \([A]_0\); second order \(t_{1/2}=1/(k[A]_0)\propto1/[A]_0\).
Given: \(t_{1/2}\) halves each time \([A]_0\) doubles.
Formula/Principle: second order: \(t_{1/2}=1/(k[A]_0)\); \(1/[A]-1/[A]_0=kt\).
Step 1: \(t_{1/2}\propto1/[A]_0\), so second order; \(k=1/(40\times0.10)=0.25\ \mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\).
Step 2: \(t=(1/0.05-1/0.20)/0.25=(20-5)/0.25=60\) s.
Why: Check with half-lives: from 0.20 M the first half-life is 20 s (to 0.10 M), and from 0.10 M the next is 40 s (to 0.05 M), total 60 s. For a second-order reaction successive half-lives double.
Why not the others: (B) A first-order half-life would not change with \([A]_0\). (C) A zero-order half-life would increase with \([A]_0\). (D) It assumes the second half-life is also 20 s, as for a first-order reaction.
Key point: \(t_{1/2}\propto[A]_0^{\,1-n}\): halves on doubling \([A]_0\) → second order.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Structure of the dichromate ion, oxidation state of chromium and the chromate–dichromate change
questions.question: Which description of the dichromate ion, \(\ce{Cr2O7^2-}\), is correct?
options: A) Two Cr atoms are joined directly by a Cr–Cr bond, each carrying three terminal oxygen atoms and a negative charge; Cr is in the +6 state

B) Two \(\ce{CrO4}\) tetrahedra share one corner oxygen, giving six equivalent terminal Cr–O bonds and two longer bridging Cr–O bonds; Cr is in the +6 state, and on adding alkali it changes to yellow chromate without any change in oxidation state
C) Two \(\ce{CrO4}\) tetrahedra share an edge (two bridging oxygens); Cr is in the +6 state, and it changes to chromate on adding acid
D) Two \(\ce{CrO4}\) tetrahedra share one corner, and all eight Cr–O bonds are equal; Cr is in the +7 state
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Two \(\ce{CrO4}\) tetrahedra share one corner oxygen, giving six equivalent terminal Cr–O bonds and two longer bridging Cr–O bonds; Cr is in the +6 state, and on adding alkali it changes to yellow chromate without any change in oxidation state.
Concept: In \(\ce{Cr2O7^2-}\) each Cr is tetrahedrally surrounded by four oxygens, and the two tetrahedra are linked by one shared oxygen (Cr–O–Cr bridge). Chromate and dichromate interconvert with pH: \(\ce{2CrO4^2- + 2H+ <=> Cr2O7^2- + H2O}\).
Why: Oxidation state: 2x + 7(−2) = −2, so x = +6. Each Cr has three terminal oxygens (6 in all), which are equivalent by resonance and shorter, and one bond to the bridging oxygen (2 in all), which is longer. Adding OH⁻ removes H⁺ and shifts the equilibrium to yellow chromate; this is an acid–base change, not a redox change.
Why not the others: (A) There is no Cr–Cr bond; the chromium atoms are linked through oxygen. (C) Only one oxygen is shared, and dichromate forms from chromate on adding acid, not the reverse. (D) Bridging and terminal Cr–O bonds differ in length, and Cr is +6, not +7.
Key point: \(\ce{Cr2O7^2-}\): corner-sharing tetrahedra, Cr(+6); orange dichromate ⇌ yellow chromate by pH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Crystal field splitting energy and observed colour from the absorption spectrum of [Ti(H2O)6]3+
questions.question: The figure shows the visible absorption spectrum of an aqueous solution of \(\ce{[Ti(H2O)6]^3+}\). Read the wavelength of maximum absorption from the figure. Which option gives the d-electron configuration of the metal ion, the colour of the solution and the crystal field splitting energy \(\Delta_o\)? (\(N_Ahc=0.1196\ \mathrm{J\,m\,mol^{-1}}\))
options: A) d¹; blue-green, the colour of the light absorbed; about 240 kJ mol⁻¹
B) d²; violet; about 240 kJ mol⁻¹
C) d¹; violet, the complementary colour of the blue-green light absorbed; about 240 kJ mol⁻¹
D) d¹; violet; about 24 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) d¹; violet, the complementary colour of the blue-green light absorbed; about 240 kJ mol⁻¹.
Concept: In an octahedral field the d orbitals split into \(t_{2g}\) (lower) and \(e_g\) (higher), separated by \(\Delta_o\). A d–d transition absorbs light of energy \(\Delta_o\); the colour seen is the complementary colour of the light absorbed.
Why: Ti is [Ar]3d²4s², so \(\ce{Ti^3+}\) is d¹ (\(t_{2g}^1\)). The peak at 498 nm (blue-green) promotes this electron to \(e_g\). Transmitted red and blue light make the solution look violet. \(\Delta_o=N_Ahc/\lambda=0.1196/(498\times10^{-9})=2.40\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\approx240\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).
Why not the others: (A) The colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed, not the same. (B) \(\ce{Ti^3+}\) has one d electron, not two. (D) It makes a power-of-ten error: 0.1196/4.98 × 10⁻⁷ is 2.4 × 10⁵ J, i.e. 240 kJ.
Key point: \(\Delta_o=N_Ahc/\lambda_{\max}\); the observed colour is complementary to the absorbed colour.
