questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Which phenols and acids release CO2 from sodium hydrogencarbonate
questions.question: Four compounds are added separately to aqueous \(\ce{NaHCO3}\): picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol, pKa 0.4), 4-nitrophenol (pKa 7.2), phenol (pKa 10.0) and benzoic acid (pKa 4.2). Carbonic acid has pKa₁ = 6.4. Which of them produce effervescence of \(\ce{CO2}\)?
options: A) Picric acid and benzoic acid only
D) Picric acid, 4-nitrophenol and benzoic acid
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Picric acid and benzoic acid only.
Concept: An acid HA releases CO₂ from hydrogencarbonate (\(\ce{HA + HCO3- -> A- + H2CO3 -> H2O + CO2}\)) only if it is a stronger acid than carbonic acid, i.e. its pKa is below about 6.4. Electron-withdrawing nitro groups at ortho and para positions stabilise the phenoxide ion and make phenols much more acidic.
Why: Picric acid (pKa 0.4) and benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) are stronger than carbonic acid and give effervescence. 4-Nitrophenol (7.2) and phenol (10.0) are weaker, so the equilibrium lies on the side of unreacted phenol and hydrogencarbonate.
Why not the others: (B) Three nitro groups make picric acid a strong acid, stronger even than benzoic acid. (C) Phenol is far too weak to decompose hydrogencarbonate; this is a standard test separating it from carboxylic acids. (D) 4-Nitrophenol, with pKa 7.2, is still weaker than carbonic acid.
Key point: CO₂ from NaHCO₃ only when pKa(acid) < pKa₁(H₂CO₃) ≈ 6.4.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Mass of precipitate and bromine consumed when phenol reacts with excess bromine water
questions.question:
0.94 g of phenol is treated with excess bromine water at room temperature, and a white precipitate forms. Molar masses are given below.

Compound | Molar mass / g mol⁻¹
Phenol | 94
4-Bromophenol | 173
2,4-Dibromophenol | 252
2,4,6-Tribromophenol | 331

What mass of precipitate forms, and how many moles of \(\ce{Br2}\) are consumed?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3.31 g of 2,4,6-tribromophenol; 0.030 mol.
Concept: The –OH group strongly activates the benzene ring and directs to the ortho and para positions. In water (a polar solvent), phenol reacts with bromine to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol, a white precipitate. In a non-polar solvent such as CS₂ at low temperature, mainly monobromophenols form.
Why: \(\ce{C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr}\). Phenol = 0.94/94 = 0.010 mol, which gives 0.010 mol of tribromophenol = 0.010 × 331 = 3.31 g. Each substitution uses one Br₂, so 3 × 0.010 = 0.030 mol of Br₂ is consumed.
Why not the others: (A) Monobromination occurs in CS₂ at low temperature, not with excess bromine water. (B) It counts half the bromine: each Br₂ supplies only one Br atom to the ring; the other forms HBr. (C) With excess bromine water all three activated positions (2, 4 and 6) are substituted.
Key point: Phenol + bromine water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white ppt) using 3 Br₂ per phenol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying an aromatic aldehyde, an aliphatic aldehyde and a methyl ketone from test results
questions.question:
Three compounds X, Y and Z are benzaldehyde, propanal and acetophenone (C₆H₅COCH₃), in some order. Their test results are shown (+ positive, − negative).

Compound | Tollens' test | Fehling's test | Iodoform test
X | + | − | −
Y | + | + | −
Z | − | − | +

Which identification is correct?
options: A) X propanal, Y benzaldehyde, Z acetophenone
B) X benzaldehyde, Y propanal, Z acetophenone
C) X benzaldehyde, Y acetophenone, Z propanal
D) X acetophenone, Y propanal, Z benzaldehyde
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) X benzaldehyde, Y propanal, Z acetophenone.
Concept: Aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens' reagent (silver mirror). Aliphatic aldehydes also reduce Fehling's solution (red Cu₂O), but aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde do not. Ketones give neither test, but methyl ketones (–COCH₃) give the iodoform test (yellow CHI₃).
Why: X is an aldehyde that fails Fehling's test → benzaldehyde. Y is an aldehyde that passes both → propanal (it has no CH₃CO– group, so no iodoform). Z is a ketone with a CH₃CO– group → acetophenone.
Why not the others: (A) Propanal reduces Fehling's solution, so it cannot be X. (C) Acetophenone is a ketone and does not give Tollens' or Fehling's test. (D) Acetophenone does not give a silver mirror, and benzaldehyde does not give iodoform.
Key point: Tollens: all aldehydes; Fehling: aliphatic aldehydes only; iodoform: CH₃CO– compounds.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linked: order of acid strength of halogen-substituted ethanoic acids and the strongest conjugate base
questions.question: Consider \(\ce{FCH2COOH}\), \(\ce{ClCH2COOH}\), \(\ce{Cl2CHCOOH}\) and \(\ce{CH3COOH}\). Which option gives the correct decreasing order of acid strength and the strongest conjugate base?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\ce{Cl2CHCOOH}>\ce{FCH2COOH}>\ce{ClCH2COOH}>\ce{CH3COOH}\); \(\ce{CH3COO-}\).
Concept: Electron-withdrawing groups (–I effect) stabilise the carboxylate ion and increase acid strength. The effect increases with the electronegativity of the halogen and with the number of halogens. The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base.
Why: Approximate pKa values: Cl₂CHCOOH 1.3, FCH₂COOH 2.6, ClCH₂COOH 2.9, CH₃COOH 4.8. One F withdraws more strongly than one Cl, but two Cl atoms withdraw more than one F. Ethanoic acid is the weakest acid, so ethanoate is the strongest conjugate base.
Why not the others: (A) Two chlorine atoms outweigh one fluorine, so dichloroethanoic acid is the strongest. (B) The strongest acid has the weakest conjugate base, so Cl₂CHCOO⁻ is the weakest base. (D) The order of acid strength is reversed.
Key point: More, and more electronegative, halogens near –COOH → stronger acid → weaker conjugate base.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ordering wavelengths of hydrogen lines from different series using the Rydberg formula
questions.question: Consider four lines of the hydrogen spectrum: P Balmer α (n = 3 → 2), Q Lyman α (n = 2 → 1), R Paschen α (n = 4 → 3) and S Balmer β (n = 4 → 2). Which is the correct increasing order of wavelength?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Q < S < P < R.
Concept: By the Bohr model, \(\dfrac1\lambda=R_H\left(\dfrac1{n_1^2}-\dfrac1{n_2^2}\right)\). A larger energy gap gives a shorter wavelength.
Given: \(R_H=1.097\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\); transitions 3→2, 2→1, 4→3, 4→2.
Formula/Principle: \(1/\lambda\propto(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)\).
Step 1: Bracket values: Q (2→1) 3/4 = 0.750; S (4→2) 3/16 = 0.1875; P (3→2) 5/36 = 0.139; R (4→3) 7/144 = 0.0486.
Step 2: Wavelengths: Q 122 nm, S 486 nm, P 656 nm, R 1875 nm.
Why: The largest bracket gives the shortest wavelength, so Q < S < P < R. Lyman lines are in the ultraviolet, Balmer lines in the visible and Paschen lines in the infrared.
Why not the others: (A) This is the decreasing order of wavelength (the order of increasing energy reversed). (B) Balmer β (4→2) has a larger energy gap than Balmer α (3→2), so its wavelength is shorter. (C) Lyman α has the largest energy gap of the four and the shortest wavelength.
Key point: Larger \((1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)\) → higher energy → shorter wavelength.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting electron gain enthalpies of O, S, F and Cl
questions.question:
The table gives the first electron gain enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹).

Element | O | S | F | Cl
\(\Delta_{eg}H\) | −141 | −200 | −328 | −349

Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The second-period elements O and F have less negative values than S and Cl because the added electron enters a small, compact 2p subshell, where electron–electron repulsion is large
B) F has a lower effective nuclear charge than Cl, so it attracts the added electron less
C) Cl has a more negative value than F because Cl is more electronegative than F
D) O and F have more electron shells than S and Cl, so the added electron is farther from the nucleus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The second-period elements O and F have less negative values than S and Cl because the added electron enters a small, compact 2p subshell, where electron–electron repulsion is large.
Concept: Electron gain enthalpy generally becomes more negative across a period and less negative down a group. The members of the second period are exceptions: because their 2p subshell is very small, an extra electron is strongly repelled by the electrons already present.
Why: Cl (−349) is more negative than F (−328), and S (−200) more negative than O (−141). In the larger 3p subshell of S and Cl the added electron feels less repulsion, so more energy is released even though the nucleus is farther away.
Why not the others: (B) F and Cl have similar effective nuclear charges for the outer electrons; the difference comes from the size of the subshell. (C) F is more electronegative than Cl, so this explanation is factually wrong. (D) O and F have fewer shells than S and Cl.
Key point: Δ_egH: Cl > F and S > O (more negative) because of repulsion in the compact 2p subshell.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Energy changes during formation of the H2 molecule in valence bond theory
questions.question: Two hydrogen atoms approach each other from a large distance to form \(\ce{H2}\). Which description is correct according to valence bond theory?
options: A) The potential energy falls continuously as the distance decreases, so the atoms would come as close as possible
B) The energy is lowest where the repulsive forces between the atoms become zero

C) Attractive forces (nucleus–electron) and repulsive forces (electron–electron and nucleus–nucleus) both act; the energy falls to a minimum at 74 pm, where they balance, and 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ is released, with the two 1s orbitals overlapping and the electron spins paired
D) A bond forms only when the two electrons have parallel spins, so that they can occupy the same region of space
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Attractive forces (nucleus–electron) and repulsive forces (electron–electron and nucleus–nucleus) both act; the energy falls to a minimum at 74 pm, where they balance, and 435.8 kJ mol⁻¹ is released, with the two 1s orbitals overlapping and the electron spins paired.
Concept: In valence bond theory, a covalent bond forms by overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals containing electrons of opposite spin. The bond length is the distance at which the potential energy of the system is a minimum.
Why: At large distance attraction dominates and the energy falls. At very short distance repulsion rises sharply. The minimum at 74 pm gives the bond length; the depth of the minimum (435.8 kJ mol⁻¹) is the bond dissociation enthalpy of H₂.
Why not the others: (A) Repulsion grows rapidly at short distances, so the energy rises again below 74 pm. (B) Repulsion is not zero at the minimum; it is balanced by attraction. (D) Electrons in the overlap region must have opposite (paired) spins, by the Pauli principle.
Key point: Bond length = distance of minimum potential energy, where attraction and repulsion balance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Total number of lone pairs on the central atoms of five molecules (VSEPR)
questions.question: What is the total number of lone pairs on the central atoms of \(\ce{ClF3}\), \(\ce{SF4}\), \(\ce{XeF2}\), \(\ce{IF5}\) and \(\ce{NH3}\), taken together?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 8.
Concept: In VSEPR theory, the number of lone pairs on the central atom = (valence electrons of the central atom − electrons used in bonds) ÷ 2. For single bonds to F or H, each bond uses one electron of the central atom.
Given: valence electrons: Cl 7, S 6, Xe 8, I 7, N 5; bonds: 3, 4, 2, 5, 3.
Formula/Principle: lone pairs = (V − number of single bonds) ÷ 2.
Step 1: ClF₃: (7 − 3)/2 = 2; SF₄: (6 − 4)/2 = 1; XeF₂: (8 − 2)/2 = 3.
Step 2: IF₅: (7 − 5)/2 = 1; NH₃: (5 − 3)/2 = 1. Total = 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 8.
Why: The shapes follow: ClF₃ T-shaped, SF₄ see-saw, XeF₂ linear, IF₅ square pyramidal and NH₃ trigonal pyramidal.
Why not the others: (A) 7 comes from taking two lone pairs on Xe in XeF₂ (that is XeF₄). (C) 9 counts two lone pairs on S in SF₄. (D) 6 misses the lone pairs on N and I.
Key point: Lone pairs on the central atom = (valence electrons − bonding electrons it supplies) ÷ 2.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Values of a parameter for which two circles touch externally or internally
questions.question: The circle \(x^2+y^2-6x-8y+k=0\) touches the circle \(x^2+y^2=1\). What are all possible values of k?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 9 and −11.
Given: \(C_1:\ x^2+y^2=1;\quad C_2:\ x^2+y^2-6x-8y+k=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{touch externally: }d=r_1+r_2;\quad \text{touch internally: }d=|r_2-r_1|\)
Step 1: \(C_1:\ \text{centre }(0,0),\ r_1=1;\quad C_2:\ \text{centre }(3,4),\ r_2=\sqrt{9+16-k}=\sqrt{25-k}\)
Step 2: \(d=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\)
Step 3: \(\text{external: }r_2+1=5\Rightarrow r_2=4\Rightarrow k=25-16=9\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{internal: }r_2-1=5\Rightarrow r_2=6\Rightarrow k=25-36=-11\quad(r_2=-4\ \text{is impossible})\]
Check: \[k=-11:\ x^2+y^2-6x-8y-11=0,\ \text{nearest point to }O\ \text{is at distance }6-5=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the unit circle lies inside the larger circle and touches it from within when }k=-11\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{misses internal contact}\); (C) \(\text{sign error in }r^2=25-k\); (D) \(\text{these are the radii, not }k\).
Key point: \(d=r_1+r_2\ \text{(external)},\ d=|r_1-r_2|\ \text{(internal)}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Limit involving an exponential and a cosine, using standard expansions
questions.question: What is the value of \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{x^2}-\cos x}{x^2}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3/2.
Given: \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{x^2}-\cos x}{x^2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\lim_{u\to0}\frac{e^u-1}{u}=1,\quad \lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}=\frac12\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\frac{e^{x^2}-\cos x}{x^2}=\frac{e^{x^2}-1}{x^2}+\frac{1-\cos x}{x^2}\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\frac{e^{x^2}-1}{x^2}\to1\ (u=x^2)\)
Worked derivation: \[L=1+\frac12=\frac32\]
Check: \[x=0.1:\ \frac{e^{0.01}-\cos0.1}{0.01}=\frac{1.010050-0.995004}{0.01}=1.5046\approx1.5\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the numerator behaves like }x^2+\tfrac{x^2}{2}=\tfrac32x^2\ \text{near }0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{only the cosine part}\); (B) \(\text{only the exponential part}\); (D) \(\text{takes }1-\cos x\sim x^2\).
Key point: \(e^{u}\approx1+u,\ \cos x\approx1-\tfrac{x^2}{2}\ \text{near }0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Correcting the mean and standard deviation after one wrongly recorded observation
questions.question: The mean and standard deviation of 10 observations were found to be 20 and 2. It was later found that one observation, 25, had been recorded as 15. What are the correct mean and standard deviation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 21 and \(\sqrt3\).
Given: \(n=10,\ \bar x=20,\ \sigma=2;\ \text{wrong value }15,\ \text{correct value }25\)
Formula/Principle: \(\textstyle\sum x=n\bar x;\quad \sum x^2=n(\sigma^2+\bar x^2);\quad \sigma^2=\frac{\sum x^2}{n}-\bar x^2\)
Step 1: \(\textstyle\sum x_{\text{wrong}}=200;\ \sum x_{\text{correct}}=200-15+25=210;\ \bar x=21\)
Step 2: \(\textstyle\sum x^2_{\text{wrong}}=10(4+400)=4040\)
Step 3: \(\textstyle\sum x^2_{\text{correct}}=4040-225+625=4440\)
Worked derivation: \[\sigma^2=\frac{4440}{10}-21^2=444-441=3,\qquad \sigma=\sqrt3\]
Check: \[\text{the change }+10\ \text{in one value raises the mean by }10/10=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{both }\textstyle\sum x\ \text{and}\ \sum x^2\ \text{must be corrected before recomputing}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{keeps the old SD}\); (C) \(\text{keeps the old mean}\); (D) \(3\ \text{is the variance, not the SD}\).
Key point: \(\textstyle\text{correct }\sum x\ \text{and }\sum x^2\ \text{first, then use }\sigma^2=\overline{x^2}-\bar x^2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Probability that the first success occurs on a given independent trial
questions.question: A fair die is thrown repeatedly. What is the probability that the first six appears on the third throw?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 25/216.
Given: \(P(\text{six})=\tfrac16,\ P(\text{not six})=\tfrac56;\ \text{throws are independent}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A\cap B\cap C)=P(A)P(B)P(C)\ \text{for independent events}\)
Step 1: \(\text{first six on 3rd throw}=\text{(not six)(not six)(six)}\)
Step 2: \(P=\tfrac56\times\tfrac56\times\tfrac16\)
Worked derivation: \[P=\frac{25}{216}\]
Check: \[\sum_{k\ge1}\left(\tfrac56\right)^{k-1}\tfrac16=\frac{1/6}{1-5/6}=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the order is fixed, so there is no factor }\binom31\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{three sixes}\); (B) \(\text{exactly one six in three throws, in any position}\); (C) \(\text{at least one six in three throws}\).
Key point: \(P(\text{first success on trial }k)=q^{k-1}p\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Theorem of total probability with a die choosing one of two bags
questions.question: A die is thrown. If it shows 1 or 2, a ball is drawn from bag I, which has 3 red and 2 black balls; otherwise a ball is drawn from bag II, which has 2 red and 4 black balls. What is the probability that the ball drawn is red?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 19/45.
Given: \(P(\text{I})=\tfrac26=\tfrac13,\ P(\text{II})=\tfrac23;\ P(R\mid\text{I})=\tfrac35,\ P(R\mid\text{II})=\tfrac26=\tfrac13\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(R)=P(\text{I})P(R\mid\text{I})+P(\text{II})P(R\mid\text{II})\)
Step 1: \(P(\text{I})P(R\mid\text{I})=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac35=\tfrac15\)
Step 2: \(P(\text{II})P(R\mid\text{II})=\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac29\)
Worked derivation: \[P(R)=\frac15+\frac29=\frac{9+10}{45}=\frac{19}{45}\]
Check: \[P(B)=\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac25+\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac23=\tfrac{2}{15}+\tfrac49=\tfrac{26}{45};\ \tfrac{19}{45}+\tfrac{26}{45}=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the bags are chosen with unequal probabilities, so each term is weighted}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes each bag with probability }\tfrac12\); (B) \(\text{pools all 11 balls}\); (D) \(\text{this is }P(\text{I}\mid R)\ \text{by Bayes' theorem}\).
Key point: \(P(R)=\sum_iP(E_i)P(R\mid E_i)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Values of a parameter for which a triangle has a given area, using a determinant
questions.question: The vertices of a triangle are \((1,2)\), \((k,4)\) and \((3,k)\), and its area is 3 square units. What is the sum of all real values of k?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3.
Given: \(\text{vertices }(1,2),(k,4),(3,k);\ \text{area}=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Area}=\tfrac12\left|\begin{vmatrix}x_1&y_1&1\\x_2&y_2&1\\x_3&y_3&1\end{vmatrix}\right|\)
Step 1: \(\begin{vmatrix}1&2&1\\k&4&1\\3&k&1\end{vmatrix}=1(4-k)-2(k-3)+1(k^2-12)=k^2-3k-2\)
Step 2: \(\tfrac12|k^2-3k-2|=3\Rightarrow k^2-3k-2=\pm6\)
Step 3: \(k^2-3k-8=0:\ \text{discriminant }9+32=41>0\Rightarrow\text{two real roots, sum }3\)
Worked derivation: \[k^2-3k+4=0:\ \text{discriminant }9-16=-7<0\Rightarrow\text{no real roots};\quad \text{sum}=3\]
Check: \[k=\tfrac{3+\sqrt{41}}2\approx4.70:\ k^2-3k-2\approx22.10-14.10-2=6\Rightarrow\text{area}=3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the modulus gives two equations, but only one has real roots}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{adds the root sums of both quadratics}\); (C) \(\text{sign error in the sum of roots}\); (D) \(\text{ignores the modulus}\).
Key point: \(\text{Area}=k\ \Rightarrow\ \det=\pm2k;\ \text{keep only real solutions}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Determinants of the adjoint and of the adjoint of the adjoint for a 3 × 3 matrix
questions.question: A is a 3 × 3 matrix with \(|A|=5\). What are \(|\operatorname{adj}A|\) and \(|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 25 and 625.
Given: \(n=3,\ |A|=5\)
Formula/Principle: \(A(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|I_n\Rightarrow|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}\)
Step 1: \(|\operatorname{adj}A|=5^{2}=25\)
Step 2: \(|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|=|\operatorname{adj}A|^{n-1}=25^2\)
Worked derivation: \[|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|=|A|^{(n-1)^2}=5^4=625\]
Check: \[A=\operatorname{diag}(5,1,1):\ \operatorname{adj}A=\operatorname{diag}(1,5,5),\ \det=25;\ \operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=\operatorname{diag}(25,5,5),\ \det=625\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{taking determinants of }A\operatorname{adj}A=|A|I\ \text{gives }|A||\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^n\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }|A|^{n-2}\); (B) \(\text{uses }|A|^{n}\ \text{for the second}\); (C) \(\text{uses }|A|^n\ \text{for the first}\).
Key point: \(|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1},\ |\operatorname{adj}\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{(n-1)^2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: First and second derivatives of a cycloid given in parametric form
questions.question: For the curve \(x=a(t-\sin t)\), \(y=a(1-\cos t)\) with \(a>0\), what are \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(t=\dfrac\pi2\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1 and \(-\dfrac1a\).
Given: \(x=a(t-\sin t),\ y=a(1-\cos t),\ t=\pi/2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt};\quad \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{dx/dt}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{a\sin t}{a(1-\cos t)}=\dfrac{2\sin\frac t2\cos\frac t2}{2\sin^2\frac t2}=\cot\dfrac t2\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\cot\dfrac t2=-\dfrac12\csc^2\dfrac t2;\quad \dfrac{dx}{dt}=2a\sin^2\dfrac t2\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\dfrac{1}{4a\sin^4\frac t2}\)
Worked derivation: \[t=\tfrac\pi2:\ \cot\tfrac\pi4=1,\quad \sin^4\tfrac\pi4=\tfrac14\Rightarrow\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-\frac{1}{4a\cdot\frac14}=-\frac1a\]
Check: \[\text{the cycloid arch is concave down everywhere }(0<t<2\pi),\ \text{so }y''<0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the second derivative needs a second division by }dx/dt\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{wrong sign}\); (C) \(\text{forgets }\sin^4(\pi/4)=1/4\); (D) \(\cot(\pi/4)=+1\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\ne\dfrac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2};\ \text{divide }\dfrac{d}{dt}(y')\ \text{by }\dfrac{dx}{dt}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Second-order differential equation satisfied by sin(log x)
questions.question: If \(y=\sin(\ln x)\) for \(x>0\), which equation does y satisfy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(x^2y''+xy'+y=0\).
Given: \(y=\sin(\ln x),\ x>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{chain rule: }\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(\ln x)=\dfrac{\cos(\ln x)}{x}\)
Step 1: \(y'=\dfrac{\cos(\ln x)}{x}\Rightarrow xy'=\cos(\ln x)\)
Step 2: \(\text{differentiate }xy'=\cos(\ln x):\ y'+xy''=-\dfrac{\sin(\ln x)}{x}\)
Worked derivation: \[x^2y''+xy'=-\sin(\ln x)=-y\ \Rightarrow\ x^2y''+xy'+y=0\]
Check: \[x=1:\ y=0,\ y'=1,\ y''=-1\ \Rightarrow\ (1)(-1)+1+0=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{with }t=\ln x,\ x\frac{d}{dx}=\frac{d}{dt},\ \text{so the equation becomes }\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}+y=0\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{at }x=1:\ -1-1+0\ne0\); (C) \(\text{at }x=e^{\pi/2}:\ y=1,\ y'=0,\ y''=-e^{-\pi},\ \text{gives }-2\ne0\); (D) \(\text{at }x=1:\ -1+0\ne0\).
Key point: \(\text{multiply }y'\ \text{by }x\ \text{before differentiating again}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Absolute maximum and minimum of a cubic on a closed interval, attained at two points each
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1\) on \([0,4]\), which statement about its absolute maximum and minimum is correct?
options: A) Maximum 5 at \(x=1\) only; minimum 1 at \(x=3\) only
C) Maximum 5 at \(x=4\) only; minimum 1 at \(x=0\) only
D) Maximum 5 at \(x=1\) and at \(x=4\); minimum 1 at \(x=0\) and at \(x=3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Maximum 5 at \(x=1\) and at \(x=4\); minimum 1 at \(x=0\) and at \(x=3\).
Given: \(f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1,\ x\in[0,4]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{compare }f\ \text{at critical points and end points}\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)=0\Rightarrow x=1,3\)
Step 2: \(f(0)=1,\ f(1)=1-6+9+1=5\)
Step 3: \(f(3)=27-54+27+1=1,\ f(4)=64-96+36+1=5\)
Worked derivation: \[\max=5\ \text{at }x=1,4;\qquad \min=1\ \text{at }x=0,3\]
Check: \[f(x)-1=x(x-3)^2\ge0\ \text{and}\ 5-f(x)=(4-x)(x-1)^2\ge0\ \text{on }[0,4]\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the local maximum equals the right end value and the local minimum equals the left end value}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the end points}\); (B) \(f\ge1\ \text{on }[0,4]\); (C) \(\text{ignores the critical points}\).
Key point: \(\text{absolute extrema on }[a,b]:\ \text{check every critical point and both ends}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting how many of four definite integrals equal π/4, using properties of definite integrals
questions.question:
Consider
\(I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\tan^3x}\), \(I_2=\displaystyle\int_0^{1}\ln\!\left(\frac1x-1\right)dx\), \(I_3=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\left(x^3\cos x+\frac{1}{2(1+x^2)}\right)dx\), \(I_4=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin^2x\,dx\).
How many of them are equal to \(\dfrac\pi4\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2.
Given: \(I_1,I_2,I_3,I_4\ \text{as defined}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\textstyle\int_0^af(x)dx=\int_0^af(a-x)dx;\quad \int_{-a}^{a}(\text{odd})=0\)
Step 1: \(I_1:\ x\to\tfrac\pi2-x\ \text{gives }\textstyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\tan^3x}{1+\tan^3x}dx;\ \text{adding, }2I_1=\tfrac\pi2\Rightarrow I_1=\tfrac\pi4\)
Step 2: \(I_2:\ \ln\frac{1-x}{x};\ x\to1-x\ \text{gives }\ln\frac{x}{1-x}=-\ln\frac{1-x}{x}\Rightarrow I_2=-I_2=0\)
Step 3: \(I_3:\ x^3\cos x\ \text{is odd}\Rightarrow I_3=\tfrac12\left[\tan^{-1}x\right]_{-1}^{1}=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac\pi2=\tfrac\pi4\)
Worked derivation: \[I_4=\int_0^\pi\frac{1-\cos2x}{2}dx=\frac\pi2\ne\frac\pi4;\qquad\text{so }I_1,I_3\ \text{only}\]
Check: \[I_1\ \text{at the midpoint }x=\tfrac\pi4:\ \text{integrand}=\tfrac12,\ \text{and the integrand is symmetric about }\tfrac12\ \text{there}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{King's property pairs }f(x)\ \text{with }f(a-x)\ \text{so that they add to a constant}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses }I_3\ \text{or }I_1\); (B) \(I_4=\pi/2\ \text{or}\ I_2=0\ \text{was counted}\); (D) \(I_2,I_4\ne\pi/4\).
Key point: \(\textstyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\tan^nx}=\frac\pi4\ \text{for every }n\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Area between an ellipse and a chord joining the ends of its semi-axes
questions.question: What is the area of the smaller region bounded by the ellipse \(\dfrac{x^2}{9}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}=1\) and the line \(\dfrac x3+\dfrac y2=1\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{3(\pi-2)}{2}\).
Given: \(\text{ellipse }a=3,\ b=2;\ \text{line through }(3,0)\ \text{and}\ (0,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Area}=\textstyle\int_0^3\left(y_{\text{ellipse}}-y_{\text{line}}\right)dx\)
Step 1: \(\textstyle\int_0^3\frac23\sqrt{9-x^2}\,dx=\frac23\cdot\frac{\pi\cdot9}{4}=\frac{3\pi}{2}\ \text{(quarter ellipse)}\)
Step 2: \(\textstyle\int_0^3\left(2-\frac{2x}{3}\right)dx=6-3=3\ \text{(right triangle)}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{Area}=\frac{3\pi}{2}-3=\frac{3(\pi-2)}{2}\approx1.71\]
Check: \[\text{quarter ellipse }\tfrac14\pi ab=\tfrac14\pi(3)(2)=\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the chord cuts off the triangle from the first-quadrant quarter of the ellipse}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{whole quarter}\); (C) \(\text{adds the triangle}\); (D) \(\text{the larger region}\ \text{is }6\pi-\tfrac{3(\pi-2)}2,\ \text{not }6\pi-3\).
Key point: \(\text{segment}=\text{quarter ellipse}-\text{triangle}=\tfrac{\pi ab}{4}-\tfrac{ab}{2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving a homogeneous differential equation with an initial condition
questions.question: Which curve is the solution of \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac yx+\tan\dfrac yx\) (for \(0<x\le1\)) that satisfies \(y(1)=\dfrac\pi2\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\sin\dfrac yx=x\).
Given: \(y'=\tfrac yx+\tan\tfrac yx,\ y(1)=\tfrac\pi2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{homogeneous: put }y=vx,\ y'=v+xv'\)
Step 1: \(v+xv'=v+\tan v\Rightarrow\cot v\,dv=\dfrac{dx}{x}\)
Step 2: \(\ln|\sin v|=\ln|x|+c\Rightarrow\sin\dfrac yx=Cx\)
Step 3: \(x=1,\ y=\tfrac\pi2:\ \sin\tfrac\pi2=C\Rightarrow C=1\)
Worked derivation: \[\sin\frac yx=x\]
Check: \[v=\sin^{-1}x:\ xv'=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=\frac{\sin v}{\cos v}=\tan v\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the substitution separates the variables}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\cos\tfrac\pi2=0\ne1\); (B) \(\tan\tfrac\pi2\ \text{is undefined}\); (C) \(\text{gives }\ln|\sin v|=-\ln x\), \(\text{wrong sign}\).
Key point: \(y'=f(y/x)\ \Rightarrow\ y=vx\ \text{makes it separable}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the sizes of two sets from the difference in their numbers of subsets
questions.question: Set A has m elements and set B has n elements. A has 112 more subsets than B. What are m and n?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) m = 7, n = 4.
Given: \(2^m-2^n=112,\ m>n\ge0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{a set with }k\ \text{elements has }2^k\ \text{subsets}\)
Step 1: \(2^n(2^{m-n}-1)=112=16\times7\)
Step 2: \(2^{m-n}-1\ \text{is odd, so }2^n=16\ \text{and}\ 2^{m-n}-1=7\)
Worked derivation: \[n=4,\quad 2^{m-4}=8\Rightarrow m=7\]
Check: \[2^7-2^4=128-16=112\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{splitting }112\ \text{into its power of 2 and odd part gives a unique answer}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(256-16=240\); (C) \(64-16=48\); (D) \(128-32=96\).
Key point: \(2^m-2^n=2^n(2^{m-n}-1):\ \text{power of 2}\times\text{odd}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Number of ordered pairs in the smallest equivalence relation containing two given pairs
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,2,3\}\). How many ordered pairs are there in the smallest equivalence relation on A that contains \((1,2)\) and \((2,3)\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 9.
Given: \(A=\{1,2,3\};\ (1,2),(2,3)\in R\)
Formula/Principle: \(R\ \text{must be reflexive, symmetric and transitive}\)
Step 1: \(\text{reflexive: }(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)\)
Step 2: \(\text{symmetric: }(2,1),(3,2)\)
Step 3: \(\text{transitive: }(1,2),(2,3)\Rightarrow(1,3);\ \text{symmetric}\Rightarrow(3,1)\)
Worked derivation: \[R=A\times A,\quad |R|=3+4+2=9\]
Check: \[\text{all three elements lie in one equivalence class, so }R=A\times A\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{equivalence relations correspond to partitions; 1, 2, 3 are forced into one class}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{reflexive + the two given pairs}\); (B) \(\text{misses transitivity}\); (D) \(\text{misses symmetry of }(1,3)\ \text{or }(2,3)\).
Key point: \(\text{linking }1\sim2\ \text{and }2\sim3\ \text{puts all three in one class}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving a trigonometric equation with the sum-to-product formula and counting solutions
questions.question: How many solutions of \(\sin5x+\sin x=\sin3x\) lie in the interval \([0,\pi]\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 6.
Given: \(\sin5x+\sin x=\sin3x,\ 0\le x\le\pi\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin C+\sin D=2\sin\dfrac{C+D}2\cos\dfrac{C-D}2\)
Step 1: \(\sin5x+\sin x=2\sin3x\cos2x\)
Step 2: \(\sin3x\,(2\cos2x-1)=0\)
Step 3: \(\sin3x=0:\ 3x=0,\pi,2\pi,3\pi\Rightarrow x=0,\tfrac\pi3,\tfrac{2\pi}3,\pi\)
Worked derivation: \[\cos2x=\tfrac12:\ 2x=\tfrac\pi3,\tfrac{5\pi}3\Rightarrow x=\tfrac\pi6,\tfrac{5\pi}6;\quad \text{total}=4+2=6\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac\pi6:\ \sin\tfrac{5\pi}6+\sin\tfrac\pi6=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1=\sin\tfrac\pi2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the two families do not share any value, so the counts add}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{only }\sin3x=0\); (C) \(\text{drops an end point}\); (D) \(\text{takes }2x\ \text{up to }4\pi\).
Key point: \(\text{factorise after sum-to-product; never cancel }\sin3x\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Parameter range for which both roots of a quadratic are real and positive
questions.question: For what values of the real number k are both roots of \(x^2-2(k-1)x+(k+5)=0\) real and positive?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(k\ge4\).
Given: \(x^2-2(k-1)x+(k+5)=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{both roots real and positive}\iff D\ge0,\ \alpha+\beta>0,\ \alpha\beta>0\)
Step 1: \(D=4(k-1)^2-4(k+5)=4(k^2-3k-4)=4(k-4)(k+1)\ge0\Rightarrow k\le-1\ \text{or}\ k\ge4\)
Step 2: \(\alpha+\beta=2(k-1)>0\Rightarrow k>1\)
Step 3: \(\alpha\beta=k+5>0\Rightarrow k>-5\)
Worked derivation: \[\{k\le-1\ \text{or}\ k\ge4\}\cap\{k>1\}\cap\{k>-5\}=\{k\ge4\}\]
Check: \[k=4:\ x^2-6x+9=(x-3)^2,\ \text{double root }3>0\ \checkmark;\quad k=-2:\ x^2+6x+3,\ \text{roots negative}\]
Why: \(\text{all three conditions must hold together}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{only }D\ge0\); (C) \(\text{only the sum condition}\); (D) \(\text{there the sum of roots is negative}\).
Key point: \(\text{real positive roots: }D\ge0,\ -b/a>0,\ c/a>0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting real roots of an equation containing x|x| by splitting into cases
questions.question: How many real roots does the equation \(x|x|-5x+6=0\) have?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3.
Given: \(x|x|-5x+6=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(|x|=x\ \text{for }x\ge0,\ |x|=-x\ \text{for }x<0\)
Step 1: \(x\ge0:\ x^2-5x+6=0\Rightarrow x=2,3\ \text{(both valid)}\)
Step 2: \(x<0:\ -x^2-5x+6=0\Rightarrow x^2+5x-6=0\Rightarrow x=1\ \text{or}\ x=-6\)
Step 3: \(x=1\ \text{is rejected (not }<0),\ x=-6\ \text{is valid}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{roots: }-6,\ 2,\ 3\ \Rightarrow\ 3\ \text{real roots}\]
Check: \[x=-6:\ (-6)(6)-5(-6)+6=-36+30+6=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each case gives a quadratic whose roots must lie in that case's range}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{only the negative root}\); (B) \(\text{only }x\ge0\); (C) \(\text{keeps the rejected }x=1\).
Key point: \(\text{split at }x=0\ \text{and check each root against its case}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the length of a word from its number of arrangements with one letter repeated, and arrangements with the repeats together
questions.question: A word has n letters: one letter occurs three times and all the other letters are different. The letters can be arranged in 840 distinct ways. What is n, and in how many of these arrangements are the three identical letters together?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) n = 7; 120.
Given: \(\text{arrangements}=\dfrac{n!}{3!}=840\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{arrangements of }n\ \text{objects with }p\ \text{alike}=\dfrac{n!}{p!}\)
Step 1: \(n!=840\times6=5040=7!\Rightarrow n=7\)
Step 2: \(\text{treat the three identical letters as one block: }7-3+1=5\ \text{units}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{arrangements with the block}=5!=120\ \ (\text{the block itself has only one internal order})\]
Check: \[\tfrac{120}{840}=\tfrac17;\ \text{direct: choose 3 consecutive places out of 7: }5\ \text{ways, others }4!=24,\ 5\times24=120\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{identical letters inside the block cannot be permuted among themselves}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{multiplies by }3!\ \text{for the block}\); (C) \(8!/6=6720\ne840\); (D) \(6!/6=120\ne840\).
Key point: \(n!/p!\ \text{for repeats; a block of identical letters counts once}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding a and n in (1 + ax)^n from two coefficients, then another coefficient
questions.question: In the expansion of \((1+ax)^n\), where n is a positive integer, the coefficients of x and \(x^2\) are 8 and 24. What is the coefficient of \(x^3\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 32.
Given: \(\binom n1a=8,\ \binom n2a^2=24\)
Formula/Principle: \(T_{r+1}=\binom nr(ax)^r\)
Step 1: \(na=8,\quad \tfrac{n(n-1)}2a^2=24\Rightarrow n(n-1)a^2=48\)
Step 2: \(\text{divide by }na=8:\ (n-1)a=6;\ \text{subtract from }na=8:\ a=2,\ n=4\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{coefficient of }x^3=\binom43a^3=4\times8=32\]
Check: \[(1+2x)^4=1+8x+24x^2+32x^3+16x^4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{two coefficients give two equations for the two unknowns}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{coefficient of }x^4\); (B) \(\text{uses }\binom43a^4\); (D) \(\text{uses }\binom42a^3=48\ \text{instead of }\binom43a^3\).
Key point: \(\text{ratio of successive coefficients: }\dfrac{T_{r+1}}{T_r}=\dfrac{n-r+1}{r}\,a\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Wave speed, fundamental frequency and the effect of tension from a standing-wave pattern on a string
questions.question: The figure shows a string of length 1.2 m, fixed at both ends, vibrating in a steady standing-wave pattern when driven at 150 Hz. Read the number of loops from the figure. What is the speed of waves on the string and its fundamental frequency? If the tension is then made four times larger, at what driving frequency will the same pattern appear?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 120 m s⁻¹; 50 Hz; 300 Hz.
Given: \(L=1.2\ \mathrm m;\ \text{3 loops (from the figure)};\ f=150\ \mathrm{Hz};\ T'=4T\)
Formula/Principle: \(L=n\dfrac\lambda2;\quad v=f\lambda;\quad v=\sqrt{T/\mu};\quad f_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L}\)
Step 1: \(n=3:\ \lambda=\dfrac{2L}{3}=0.80\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(v=150\times0.80=120\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\quad f_1=\dfrac{v}{2L}=\dfrac{120}{2.4}=50\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
Step 3: \(T\to4T\Rightarrow v\to\sqrt4\,v=240\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{same 3-loop pattern: }\lambda=0.80\ \mathrm m\Rightarrow f'=\frac{240}{0.80}=300\ \mathrm{Hz}\]
Check: \[f_3=3f_1=150\ \mathrm{Hz}\ \checkmark;\quad f'_3=3\times\frac{240}{2.4}=300\ \mathrm{Hz}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the pattern fixes }\lambda;\ \text{the tension fixes }v;\ \text{so }f\propto\sqrt T\ \text{for a given pattern}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes }f\propto T\ \text{instead of}\ \sqrt T\); (C) \(\text{takes the whole string as one wavelength}\); (D) \(\text{takes one loop as a full wavelength}\).
Key point: \(\text{each loop}=\lambda/2;\ v=\sqrt{T/\mu}\Rightarrow f\propto\sqrt T\)
questions.image_alt: A horizontal string 1.2 m long fixed between two clamps, vibrating in a standing wave with three equal loops; nodes are marked at both clamps and at two points in between, and the label "150 Hz" is next to the vibrator.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Electric field inside and outside a uniformly charged solid sphere and flux through an inner Gaussian sphere
questions.question: A non-conducting solid sphere of radius R carries charge Q spread uniformly through its volume. The electric field at its surface is \(E_0\). What is the field at distance \(R/2\) from the centre, the field at distance 2R, and the electric flux through a concentric spherical surface of radius \(R/2\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(E_0/2\); \(E_0/4\); \(Q/(8\varepsilon_0)\).
Given: \(\text{uniform volume charge }Q,\ \text{radius }R;\ E(R)=E_0=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0R^2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Gauss's law: }\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 1: \(r=\tfrac R2:\ q_{\text{enc}}=Q\left(\tfrac{r}{R}\right)^3=\tfrac Q8\)
Step 2: \(E\cdot4\pi\left(\tfrac R2\right)^2=\dfrac{Q/8}{\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow E=\dfrac{Q}{8\pi\varepsilon_0R^2}=\dfrac{E_0}{2}\)
Step 3: \(r=2R:\ E=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(2R)^2}=\dfrac{E_0}4\)
Worked derivation: \[\Phi\left(\tfrac R2\right)=\frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}=\frac{Q}{8\varepsilon_0}\]
Check: \[\text{inside: }E=\frac{Qr}{4\pi\varepsilon_0R^3}\propto r\ \Rightarrow E(R/2)=E_0/2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{inside, only the charge within radius }r\ \text{contributes; outside, the sphere acts as a point charge}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{treats the whole charge as enclosed at }R/2\); (B) \(\text{takes }q_{\text{enc}}\propto r\ \text{and }E\propto1/r\); (C) \(\text{this is for a conductor, where charge lies on the surface}\).
Key point: \(\text{uniform solid sphere: }E\propto r\ \text{inside},\ E\propto1/r^2\ \text{outside}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Common potential and loss of energy when two charged capacitors are joined, like plates together
questions.question: A 2.0 µF capacitor is charged to 100 V and a 4.0 µF capacitor is charged to 50 V. They are disconnected from their supplies and then joined, positive plate to positive plate and negative to negative. What is the final common potential difference, and how much electrostatic energy is lost?
options: A) 75 V; no energy is lost
B) 66.7 V; no energy is lost
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 66.7 V; about 1.67 mJ.
Given: \(C_1=2.0\ \mu\mathrm F,\ V_1=100\ \mathrm V;\ C_2=4.0\ \mu\mathrm F,\ V_2=50\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{charge is conserved: }V=\dfrac{C_1V_1+C_2V_2}{C_1+C_2};\quad U=\tfrac12CV^2\)
Step 1: \(q=2.0\times100+4.0\times50=400\ \mu\mathrm C;\quad V=\dfrac{400}{6.0}=66.7\ \mathrm V\)
Step 2: \(U_i=\tfrac12(2.0\times10^{-6})(100)^2+\tfrac12(4.0\times10^{-6})(50)^2=0.0100+0.0050=0.0150\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(U_f=\tfrac12(6.0\times10^{-6})(66.7)^2=0.01333\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta U=\frac{C_1C_2(V_1-V_2)^2}{2(C_1+C_2)}=\frac{(2\times4)\times10^{-12}\times2500}{2\times6\times10^{-6}}=1.67\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[U_i-U_f=0.0150-0.01333=0.00167\ \mathrm J\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{charge flows from the higher-potential capacitor; energy is lost as heat and radiation in the wires}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{averages the voltages without weighting by }C\); (B) \(\text{energy is always lost when }V_1\ne V_2\); (D) \(\text{this happens if opposite plates are joined: the equal charges of }200\ \mu\mathrm C\ \text{cancel and all 15 mJ is lost}\).
Key point: \(\text{charge conserved, energy not: loss}=\dfrac{C_1C_2(V_1-V_2)^2}{2(C_1+C_2)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Time to boil water using two identical heating coils in series and in parallel
questions.question: An electric kettle has two identical heating coils. With one coil connected to the mains, a certain quantity of water boils in 10 min. How long does the same quantity of water, starting at the same temperature, take to boil when both coils are connected in series, and when they are connected in parallel, to the same mains? Neglect heat losses and the change of resistance with temperature.
options: A) 20 min in series; 5 min in parallel
B) 5 min in series; 20 min in parallel
C) 20 min in series; 10 min in parallel
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 20 min in series; 5 min in parallel.
Given: \(\text{one coil: resistance }R,\ t_1=10\ \text{min};\ \text{same supply voltage }V\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=\dfrac{V^2}{R_{\text{eq}}};\quad Pt=\text{heat needed (fixed)}\Rightarrow t\propto R_{\text{eq}}\)
Step 1: \(\text{series: }R_{\text{eq}}=2R\Rightarrow P=\dfrac{V^2}{2R}\)
Step 2: \(\text{parallel: }R_{\text{eq}}=\dfrac R2\Rightarrow P=\dfrac{2V^2}{R}\)
Worked derivation: \[t_s=10\times\frac{2R}{R}=20\ \text{min},\qquad t_p=10\times\frac{R/2}{R}=5\ \text{min}\]
Check: \[P_p:P_1:P_s=4:2:1\ \ \text{(in units of }V^2/2R)\ \Rightarrow\ t=5:10:20\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at fixed voltage, lower resistance draws more current and gives more power}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses }P=I^2R\ \text{at fixed current, but the voltage is fixed}\); (C) \(\text{parallel doubles the power, halving the time}\); (D) \(\text{power depends on the connection}\).
Key point: \(\text{fixed }V:\ P=V^2/R\ \Rightarrow\ \text{parallel heats fastest}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Force between two parallel currents (Newton's third law) and the neutral point between them
questions.question: Two long, straight, parallel wires are 10 cm apart in air and carry currents of 5.0 A and 10 A in the same direction. What is the force per metre on each wire, and where is the magnetic field zero? (\(\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}\))
options: A) \(1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\), repulsive; outside the wires, 3.3 cm beyond the 5.0 A wire
B) \(2.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\) on the 10 A wire and \(1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\) on the 5.0 A wire, attractive; between the wires, midway
C) \(1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\), attractive; between the wires, 6.7 cm from the 5.0 A wire
D) \(1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\) on each wire, attractive, equal and opposite; between the wires, 3.3 cm from the 5.0 A wire
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\) on each wire, attractive, equal and opposite; between the wires, 3.3 cm from the 5.0 A wire.
Given: \(I_1=5.0\ \mathrm A,\ I_2=10\ \mathrm A\ \text{(same direction)};\ d=0.10\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d};\quad B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2\pi r}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{2\times10^{-7}\times5.0\times10}{0.10}=1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(\text{same direction}\Rightarrow\text{attraction; by Newton's third law the forces are equal and opposite}\)
Step 3: \(\text{between the wires the two fields are opposite: }\dfrac{I_1}{x}=\dfrac{I_2}{0.10-x}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{5}{x}=\frac{10}{0.10-x}\Rightarrow0.50-5x=10x\Rightarrow x=0.033\ \mathrm m=3.3\ \mathrm{cm}\]
Check: \[B_1=\frac{2\times10^{-7}\times5}{0.0333}=3.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm T=B_2=\frac{2\times10^{-7}\times10}{0.0667}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each wire sits in the other's field; the force formula is symmetric in }I_1,I_2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{like currents attract, and outside the wires the fields add}\); (B) \(\text{violates Newton's third law}\); (C) \(\text{the neutral point is nearer the weaker current}\).
Key point: \(\text{parallel currents attract with equal forces; }B=0\ \text{nearer the smaller current}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Motional emf, retarding force and energy conservation for a rod moved along rails
questions.question: A metal rod of length 0.40 m slides at a constant 5.0 m s⁻¹ along two parallel frictionless rails joined at one end by a 2.0 Ω resistor. The arrangement is in a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The resistances of the rod and rails are negligible. What are the induced emf, the external force needed to keep the speed constant, and the power delivered by this force?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1.0 V; 0.10 N; 0.50 W.
Given: \(B=0.50\ \mathrm T,\ l=0.40\ \mathrm m,\ v=5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ R=2.0\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon=Blv;\quad I=\varepsilon/R;\quad F=BIl;\quad P=Fv\)
Step 1: \(\varepsilon=0.50\times0.40\times5.0=1.0\ \mathrm V\)
Step 2: \(I=1.0/2.0=0.50\ \mathrm A;\quad F=0.50\times0.50\times0.40=0.10\ \mathrm N\)
Worked derivation: \[P_{\text{mech}}=Fv=0.10\times5.0=0.50\ \mathrm W\]
Check: \[P_{\text{elec}}=I^2R=0.25\times2.0=0.50\ \mathrm W=P_{\text{mech}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{by Lenz's law the magnetic force opposes the motion; the work done against it appears as heat in }R\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }\tfrac12I^2R\); (C) \(\text{leaves out the length in }F=BIl\); (D) \(\text{doubles the current}\).
Key point: \(F=\dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R};\quad Fv=I^2R\ \text{(energy conservation)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Impedance, current, power factor and power in a series LCR circuit
questions.question: A series circuit has a 40 Ω resistor, an inductor of reactance 50 Ω and a capacitor of reactance 20 Ω, connected to a 250 V (rms) AC supply. What are the rms current, the power factor, the average power and the phase of the current relative to the voltage?
options: A) 5.0 A; 0.80; 1000 W; current lags the voltage
B) 5.0 A; 0.80; 1250 W; current lags the voltage
C) 3.1 A; 0.50; 385 W; current lags the voltage
D) 5.0 A; 0.60; 750 W; current leads the voltage
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 5.0 A; 0.80; 1000 W; current lags the voltage.
Given: \(R=40\ \Omega,\ X_L=50\ \Omega,\ X_C=20\ \Omega,\ V=250\ \mathrm V\ \text{(rms)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2};\quad I=V/Z;\quad \cos\phi=R/Z;\quad P=I^2R\)
Step 1: \(Z=\sqrt{40^2+30^2}=50\ \Omega;\quad I=250/50=5.0\ \mathrm A\)
Step 2: \(\cos\phi=40/50=0.80\)
Worked derivation: \[P=VI\cos\phi=250\times5.0\times0.80=1000\ \mathrm W=I^2R=25\times40\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[\tan\phi=\frac{X_L-X_C}{R}=\frac{30}{40}=0.75>0\Rightarrow\text{inductive},\ \text{current lags}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{only the resistor dissipates power; the net reactance is inductive}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses }VI\ \text{without the power factor}\); (C) \(\text{adds the reactances: }Z=\sqrt{40^2+70^2}\approx81\ \Omega\); (D) \(\text{swaps }R/Z\ \text{with }X/Z\ \text{and the sign}\).
Key point: \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2};\ X_L>X_C\Rightarrow\text{current lags}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Power of two thin lenses in contact and separated by a distance
questions.question: A thin convex lens of focal length 25 cm and a thin concave lens of focal length 50 cm have a common axis. What is the power of the combination when they are in contact, and when they are 25 cm apart?
options: B) +6 D in contact; +4 D when 25 cm apart
C) +2 D in contact; +4 D when 25 cm apart
D) −2 D in contact; 0 D when 25 cm apart
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) +2 D in contact; +4 D when 25 cm apart.
Given: \(f_1=+0.25\ \mathrm m\Rightarrow P_1=+4\ \mathrm D;\ f_2=-0.50\ \mathrm m\Rightarrow P_2=-2\ \mathrm D;\ d=0.25\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=P_1+P_2\ \text{(contact)};\quad P=P_1+P_2-dP_1P_2\ \text{(separated)}\)
Step 1: \(\text{contact: }P=4-2=+2\ \mathrm D\ (f=+50\ \mathrm{cm})\)
Step 2: \(\text{separated: }dP_1P_2=0.25\times4\times(-2)=-2\)
Worked derivation: \[P=4-2-(-2)=+4\ \mathrm D\ (f=+25\ \mathrm{cm})\]
Check: \[\frac1F=\frac1{f_1}+\frac1{f_2}-\frac{d}{f_1f_2}=4-2-\frac{0.25}{(0.25)(-0.50)}=4-2+2=4\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{separation changes the power when one lens is converging and the other diverging}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the separation term}\); (B) \(\text{adds magnitudes of powers}\); (D) \(\text{sign of the convex lens reversed}\).
Key point: \(P=P_1+P_2-dP_1P_2\ \text{(}d\ \text{in metres)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Work function, stopping potential at a second wavelength and threshold wavelength from a photocell experiment
questions.question: In a photocell experiment, light of wavelength 248 nm falls on a metal surface and the photocurrent just stops when the collector is 2.0 V negative with respect to the emitter. The light is replaced by light of wavelength 310 nm. What is the new stopping potential, and what is the threshold wavelength of the metal? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1.0 V; 413 nm.
Given: \(\lambda_1=248\ \mathrm{nm},\ V_1=2.0\ \mathrm V;\ \lambda_2=310\ \mathrm{nm};\ hc=1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(eV_0=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}-\phi;\quad \lambda_0=\dfrac{hc}{\phi}\)
Step 1: \(E_1=1240/248=5.0\ \mathrm{eV};\ \phi=5.0-2.0=3.0\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Step 2: \(E_2=1240/310=4.0\ \mathrm{eV};\ V_2=4.0-3.0=1.0\ \mathrm V\)
Worked derivation: \[\lambda_0=\frac{1240}{3.0}=413\ \mathrm{nm}\]
Check: \[310<413\ \mathrm{nm},\ \text{so emission still occurs}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the work function is a property of the metal, so it is found from one reading and used for the other}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes }\phi=2.0\ \mathrm{eV}\ \text{(the stopping potential)}\); (C) \(\text{scales }V_0\ \text{in proportion to }1/\lambda\ \text{ignoring }\phi\); (D) \(\text{assumes }V_0\ \text{is independent of }\lambda\).
Key point: \(eV_0=hc/\lambda-\phi;\ \phi\ \text{is fixed for the metal}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Level reached by a hydrogen atom absorbing a photon, and the number of emission lines that follow
questions.question: A hydrogen atom in its ground state absorbs a photon of energy 12.75 eV. To which level is it excited, and how many different spectral lines can appear as it returns to the ground state, possibly in several steps?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) n = 4; 6 lines.
Given: \(E_n=-\dfrac{13.6}{n^2}\ \mathrm{eV};\ E_{\text{photon}}=12.75\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{energy conservation: }E_n=E_1+E_{\text{photon}};\ \text{number of lines}=\dfrac{n(n-1)}2\)
Step 1: \(E_n=-13.6+12.75=-0.85\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Step 2: \(n^2=13.6/0.85=16\Rightarrow n=4\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{lines}=\frac{4\times3}{2}=6:\ 4\to3,\ 4\to2,\ 4\to1,\ 3\to2,\ 3\to1,\ 2\to1\]
Check: \[E_4-E_1=13.6\left(1-\tfrac1{16}\right)=12.75\ \mathrm{eV}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the photon energy matches exactly the gap from }n=1\ \text{to}\ n=4\)
Why not the others: (B) \(E_3-E_1=12.09\ \mathrm{eV}\); (C) \(\text{counts only jumps ending at }n=1\); (D) \(E_5-E_1=13.06\ \mathrm{eV}\).
Key point: \(\text{from level }n:\ \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}\ \text{possible lines}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Fission rate and daily fuel consumption of a 1 MW reactor
questions.question: Each fission of a uranium-235 nucleus releases about 200 MeV. A reactor produces 1.0 MW of power from fission. About how many fissions occur per second, and what mass of uranium-235 is used up per day? (1 MeV = \(1.6\times10^{-13}\) J; \(N_A=6.0\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(3.1\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\); about 1.05 g.
Given: \(P=1.0\times10^{6}\ \mathrm W;\ E=200\ \mathrm{MeV}=3.2\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm J;\ M=235\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{fissions per second}=P/E;\ \text{mass}=\dfrac{N}{N_A}\times M\)
Step 1: \(\text{rate}=\dfrac{1.0\times10^6}{3.2\times10^{-11}}=3.1\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(N_{\text{day}}=3.1\times10^{16}\times86400=2.7\times10^{21}\)
Worked derivation: \[m=\frac{2.7\times10^{21}}{6.0\times10^{23}}\times235=4.5\times10^{-3}\times235\approx1.05\ \mathrm g\]
Check: \[1.05\ \mathrm g\times\frac{6.0\times10^{23}}{235}\times3.2\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm J\approx8.6\times10^{10}\ \mathrm J=1.0\ \mathrm{MW}\times86400\ \mathrm s\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{fission releases about a million times more energy per atom than chemical burning}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }1\ \mathrm{MeV}=1.6\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm J\); (B) \(\text{uses 200 keV instead of 200 MeV}\); (D) \(\text{stops at moles and forgets }\times235\).
Key point: \(\text{about 1 g of U-235 per MW-day}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Current in a circuit with two silicon diodes in opposite branches, for both battery polarities
questions.question: A 10 V battery is connected in series with a 1.0 kΩ resistor to a pair of parallel branches. Branch 1 has a silicon diode \(D_1\) in series with a 2.0 kΩ resistor; branch 2 has a silicon diode \(D_2\), pointing the opposite way, in series with a 1.0 kΩ resistor. With the battery connected so that \(D_1\) is forward biased, what current flows from the battery? What is the current when the battery is reversed? Take the forward voltage of a conducting silicon diode as 0.7 V and its reverse current as zero.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3.1 mA; 4.65 mA.
Given: \(V=10\ \mathrm V;\ R_s=1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega};\ \text{branch 1: }D_1+2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega};\ \text{branch 2: }D_2\ (\text{reversed})+1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega};\ V_D=0.7\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{a reverse-biased diode carries no current; a forward one drops }0.7\ \mathrm V\)
Step 1: \(\text{first polarity: }D_2\ \text{is off, only branch 1 conducts}\)
Step 2: \(I=\dfrac{10-0.7}{1.0+2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}}=\dfrac{9.3}{3.0\times10^3}=3.1\ \mathrm{mA}\)
Step 3: \(\text{reversed: }D_1\ \text{is off, }D_2\ \text{conducts}\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\frac{10-0.7}{1.0+1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}}=\frac{9.3}{2.0\times10^3}=4.65\ \mathrm{mA}\]
Check: \[\text{first case: }V_{2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}=6.2\ \mathrm V,\ V_{1\,\mathrm{k\Omega}}=3.1\ \mathrm V,\ 6.2+3.1+0.7=10\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each diode acts as a switch that selects one branch for each polarity}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the 0.7 V drop}\); (B) \(D_2\ \text{conducts when the battery is reversed}\); (C) \(\text{the two cases are swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{ideal-plus-0.7 V model: off}=\text{open},\ \text{on}=0.7\ \mathrm V\ \text{source}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Displacement, distance, average velocity and average speed from a velocity–time graph that crosses zero
questions.question: The figure shows the velocity–time graph of a body moving along a straight line for 16 s. Read the values from the graph. What are the displacement, the distance travelled, the average velocity and the average speed for the whole 16 s?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 76 m; 84 m; 4.75 m s⁻¹; 5.25 m s⁻¹.
Given: \(\text{from the graph: }(0,0)\to(4,8)\to(10,8)\to(14,0)\to(16,-4)\ \ (t\ \text{in s},\ v\ \text{in m\,s}^{-1})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{displacement}=\text{signed area under }v\text{–}t;\ \text{distance}=\text{total area (all positive)}\)
Step 1: \(0\text{–}4\ \mathrm s:\ \tfrac12(4)(8)=16\ \mathrm m;\quad 4\text{–}10\ \mathrm s:\ 6\times8=48\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(10\text{–}14\ \mathrm s:\ \tfrac12(4)(8)=16\ \mathrm m;\quad 14\text{–}16\ \mathrm s:\ \tfrac12(2)(-4)=-4\ \mathrm m\)
Step 3: \(\text{displacement}=16+48+16-4=76\ \mathrm m;\ \text{distance}=16+48+16+4=84\ \mathrm m\)
Worked derivation: \[\bar v=\frac{76}{16}=4.75\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad \text{average speed}=\frac{84}{16}=5.25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[\text{the slope from }10\ \text{to}\ 16\ \mathrm s\ \text{is constant: }-8/4=-12/6=-2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\ \text{so the line is straight through }v=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{after }14\ \mathrm s\ \text{the body moves backwards, which reduces displacement but adds to distance}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{treats the backward 4 m as forward}\); (C) \(\text{subtracts the backward motion from the distance}\); (D) \(\text{ignores the last 2 s for displacement}\).
Key point: \(\text{signed area}=\text{displacement};\ \text{total area}=\text{distance}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Launch speed and landing velocity of a ball rolling off a table, from its height and range
questions.question: A ball rolls off the edge of a horizontal table 1.25 m high and lands on the floor 2.0 m from the foot of the table. Neglect air resistance and take g = 10 m s⁻². With what speed did it leave the table, and what is its velocity just before it lands?
options: A) 4.0 m s⁻¹; 5.0 m s⁻¹ at about 51° below the horizontal
B) 4.0 m s⁻¹; 6.4 m s⁻¹ at about 51° below the horizontal
C) 8.0 m s⁻¹; 9.4 m s⁻¹ at about 32° below the horizontal
D) 4.0 m s⁻¹; 6.4 m s⁻¹ at about 39° below the horizontal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 4.0 m s⁻¹; 6.4 m s⁻¹ at about 51° below the horizontal.
Given: \(h=1.25\ \mathrm m,\ R=2.0\ \mathrm m,\ g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\ u_y=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(h=\tfrac12gt^2;\quad R=u\,t;\quad v_y=gt\)
Step 1: \(t=\sqrt{2h/g}=\sqrt{0.25}=0.50\ \mathrm s\)
Step 2: \(u=R/t=2.0/0.50=4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\quad v_y=10\times0.50=5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Worked derivation: \[v=\sqrt{4.0^2+5.0^2}=\sqrt{41}=6.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad \tan\theta=\frac{5.0}{4.0}\Rightarrow\theta\approx51^\circ\ \text{below horizontal}\]
Check: \[\text{energy: }v^2=u^2+2gh=16+25=41\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{horizontal and vertical motions are independent; the time is set by the height alone}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{gives only the vertical component as the speed}\); (C) \(\text{uses }t=0.25\ \mathrm s\); (D) \(\text{angle measured from the vertical}\).
Key point: \(\text{horizontal launch: }t=\sqrt{2h/g},\ u=R/t\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Minimum speed and tensions for a stone whirled in a complete vertical circle
questions.question: A stone of mass 0.20 kg is tied to a light string 0.40 m long and whirled in a vertical circle. What is the minimum speed at the lowest point for the stone to complete the circle, the tension at the lowest point at this speed, and the speed at the highest point? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4.5 m s⁻¹; 12 N; 2.0 m s⁻¹.
Given: \(m=0.20\ \mathrm{kg},\ L=0.40\ \mathrm m,\ g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{top (critical): }T=0,\ mg=\dfrac{mv_t^2}{L};\ \text{energy: }v_b^2=v_t^2+4gL\)
Step 1: \(v_t=\sqrt{gL}=\sqrt{4.0}=2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(v_b=\sqrt{5gL}=\sqrt{20}=4.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Worked derivation: \[T_b=mg+\frac{mv_b^2}{L}=0.20\times10+\frac{0.20\times20}{0.40}=2.0+10=12\ \mathrm N=6mg\]
Check: \[\tfrac12mv_b^2-\tfrac12mv_t^2=\tfrac12(0.20)(20-4)=1.6\ \mathrm J=mg(2L)=0.20\times10\times0.80\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at the top the string can only pull, so gravity alone must supply the centripetal force at the minimum speed}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses the top speed at the bottom}\); (B) \(\text{forgets the weight in }T_b\); (C) \(\text{uses }\sqrt{2gL},\ \text{which only reaches the top with zero speed, so the string goes slack before that}\).
Key point: \(v_{\text{bottom,min}}=\sqrt{5gL};\ T_{\text{bottom}}=6mg\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Energy needed to place a satellite in a circular orbit at height equal to the Earth's radius
questions.question: A satellite of mass m is to be placed in a circular orbit at a height equal to the Earth's radius R above the surface. Ignoring the Earth's rotation and air resistance, what is the increase in its gravitational potential energy, its kinetic energy in orbit, and the total energy that must be supplied? (g is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface.)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) mgR/2; mgR/4; 3mgR/4.
Given: \(r_1=R,\ r_2=2R;\ GM=gR^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r};\quad K_{\text{orbit}}=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\)
Step 1: \(\Delta U=-\dfrac{GMm}{2R}+\dfrac{GMm}{R}=\dfrac{GMm}{2R}=\dfrac{mgR}{2}\)
Step 2: \(K=\dfrac{GMm}{2(2R)}=\dfrac{GMm}{4R}=\dfrac{mgR}{4}\)
Worked derivation: \[E_{\text{supplied}}=\Delta U+K=\frac{mgR}2+\frac{mgR}4=\frac{3mgR}4\]
Check: \[E_{\text{final}}-E_{\text{initial}}=-\frac{GMm}{4R}-\left(-\frac{GMm}{R}\right)=\frac{3GMm}{4R}=\frac{3mgR}4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(mgh\ \text{overestimates }\Delta U\ \text{because }g\ \text{falls with height}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }mgh\ \text{with constant }g\); (B) \(\text{orbital KE at }2R\ \text{is }GMm/4R\); (D) \(\Delta U\ \text{is }GMm/2R,\ \text{not }/4R\).
Key point: \(\text{orbit: }K=-E=-U/2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Scaling of terminal velocity and viscous force with radius and viscosity (Stokes' law)
questions.question: A steel ball of radius 1.0 mm falls through liquid L₁ with terminal velocity 1.0 cm s⁻¹. A steel ball of radius 0.50 mm falls through liquid L₂, which has the same density as L₁ but half its viscosity. What is the terminal velocity of the small ball, and what is the ratio of the viscous force on the small ball to that on the large ball, each at its terminal velocity?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.50 cm s⁻¹; 1/8.
Given: \(r_1=1.0\ \mathrm{mm},\ v_1=1.0\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}},\ \eta_1;\ r_2=0.50\ \mathrm{mm},\ \eta_2=\eta_1/2;\ \text{same densities}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta};\quad F_{\text{viscous}}=6\pi\eta rv_t=\text{weight}-\text{buoyancy}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{v_2}{v_1}=\left(\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}\right)^2\dfrac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}=\dfrac14\times2=\dfrac12\Rightarrow v_2=0.50\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 2: \(\text{at terminal velocity }F=\tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho-\sigma)g\propto r^3\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{F_2}{F_1}=\left(\frac{0.50}{1.0}\right)^3=\frac18\]
Check: \[\frac{F_2}{F_1}=\frac{\eta_2r_2v_2}{\eta_1r_1v_1}=\frac12\times\frac12\times\frac12=\frac18\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at terminal velocity the drag balances the net weight, which depends only on volume}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{ignores the change in viscosity}\); (C) \(\text{takes }v_t\ \text{independent of }r\); (D) \(\text{takes drag }\propto r^2\).
Key point: \(v_t\propto r^2/\eta;\ \text{drag at terminal velocity}\propto r^3\)

questions.sub_topic: Ratio of thermal conductivities from wax melted along rods, and the junction temperature of the two rods in series
questions.question: Two rods X and Y of the same length and cross-section are coated with wax and have one end dipped in boiling water. In the steady state, the wax melts to a distance of 5.0 cm along X and 10.0 cm along Y. The same rods are then joined end to end, with the free end of X at 100 °C and the free end of Y at 0 °C, and the sides insulated. What is the ratio of thermal conductivities \(K_X:K_Y\), and what is the steady temperature of the junction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1 : 4; 20 °C.
Given: \(l_X=5.0\ \mathrm{cm},\ l_Y=10.0\ \mathrm{cm};\ \text{series: }100\ ^\circ\mathrm C\ (X\ \text{end}),\ 0\ ^\circ\mathrm C\ (Y\ \text{end})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Ingen-Hausz: }K\propto l^2;\quad \text{series: }K_XA\dfrac{100-T}{L}=K_YA\dfrac{T-0}{L}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{K_X}{K_Y}=\left(\dfrac{5.0}{10.0}\right)^2=\dfrac14\)
Step 2: \(K_X(100-T)=4K_X\,T\)
Worked derivation: \[100-T=4T\Rightarrow T=20\ ^\circ\mathrm C\]
Check: \[\text{temperature drops: }80\ ^\circ\mathrm C\ \text{across X},\ 20\ ^\circ\mathrm C\ \text{across Y};\ K_X\times80=K_Y\times20\ \Rightarrow\ \tfrac{K_X}{K_Y}=\tfrac14\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the same heat current flows through both rods, so the poorer conductor has the larger temperature drop}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes }K\propto l\); (B) \(\text{gives the temperature drop across X instead of the junction temperature}\); (D) \(\text{inverts the ratio}\).
Key point: \(\text{wax length}\propto\sqrt K;\ \text{series rods: larger drop across the poorer conductor}\)

questions.sub_topic: Work and rejected heat of a Carnot engine, and the reservoir changes needed for a higher efficiency
questions.question: A Carnot engine works between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K and absorbs 1000 J from the hot reservoir per cycle. How much work does it do per cycle, and how much heat does it reject? To raise the efficiency to 50 %, what sink temperature (with the source unchanged) or what source temperature (with the sink unchanged) is needed?
options: A) 400 J and 600 J; sink 250 K or source 750 K
B) 600 J and 400 J; sink 250 K or source 600 K
C) 400 J and 600 J; sink 150 K or source 600 K
D) 400 J and 600 J; sink 250 K or source 600 K
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 400 J and 600 J; sink 250 K or source 600 K.
Given: \(T_1=500\ \mathrm K,\ T_2=300\ \mathrm K,\ Q_1=1000\ \mathrm J;\ \eta'=0.50\)
Formula/Principle: \(\eta=1-\dfrac{T_2}{T_1};\quad W=\eta Q_1;\quad Q_1=W+Q_2\ \text{(energy conservation)}\)
Step 1: \(\eta=1-\dfrac{300}{500}=0.40;\ W=400\ \mathrm J;\ Q_2=1000-400=600\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(\text{sink: }1-\dfrac{T_2'}{500}=0.50\Rightarrow T_2'=250\ \mathrm K\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{source: }1-\frac{300}{T_1'}=0.50\Rightarrow T_1'=600\ \mathrm K\]
Check: \[\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}=\frac{600}{1000}=\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{300}{500}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the Carnot efficiency depends only on the ratio of reservoir temperatures}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{750 K gives }\eta=0.60\); (B) \(\text{swaps }W\ \text{and}\ Q_2\); (C) \(\text{150 K gives }\eta=0.70\).
Key point: \(\eta_{\text{Carnot}}=1-T_2/T_1;\ Q_1=W+Q_2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Effect of buoyancy, a draining hollow bob, amplitude and altitude on the period of a simple pendulum
questions.question:
Consider these statements about a simple pendulum making small oscillations.
I. If its bob, of density \(8000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), oscillates fully immersed in water (density \(1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)), neglecting viscous drag, the period becomes \(\sqrt{8/7}\) times the period in air.
II. If the bob is a hollow sphere full of water that slowly drains out through a small hole at the bottom, the period first increases and then returns to its original value.
III. Doubling the (still small) amplitude doubles the period.
IV. At a height above the Earth's surface equal to the Earth's radius, the period is twice its value at the surface.
Which statements are correct?
options: B) I, II and IV only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) I, II and IV only.
Given: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{l/g_{\text{eff}}};\ \rho_{\text{bob}}=8000,\ \rho_{\text{water}}=1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{period depends on the effective length (to the centre of mass) and on }g_{\text{eff}}\)
Step 1: \(\text{I: }g_{\text{eff}}=g\left(1-\tfrac{1000}{8000}\right)=\tfrac78g\Rightarrow T'=T\sqrt{8/7}\)
Step 2: \(\text{II: as water drains, the centre of mass first moves down (}l\ \text{increases) and then back up to the centre when empty}\)
Step 3: \(\text{III: for small oscillations }T\ \text{is independent of amplitude}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{IV: }g_h=\frac{g}{(1+h/R)^2}=\frac g4\Rightarrow T_h=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g/4}}=2T\]
Check: \[\text{I: net downward force }=(\rho-\sigma)Vg=\tfrac78\rho Vg\ \text{on mass }\rho V\Rightarrow g_{\text{eff}}=\tfrac78g\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{buoyancy reduces the restoring force but not the inertia, so the pendulum slows}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{III is false and II, IV are true}\); (C) \(\text{III is false and I is true}\); (D) \(\text{II is also true}\).
Key point: \(T\propto\sqrt{l_{\text{cm}}/g_{\text{eff}}},\ \text{independent of small amplitude}\)
